title: Ravens Red Zone Report: What’s Working And Failing And What Must Change in Week 8
full_text:
There is so much going on with the Ravens at a macro level right now between coaches and general managers getting exposed and all the second-half collapses and blaming fans for not being loud enough and with team legends excoriating this current edition on social media, it’s easy to gloss over specific micro issues.
And, with two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson coming back from a three-week absence due to a high-ankle sprain, it’s also easy to fall into the trap that he’s going to just solve everything. Indeed, he is the ultimate deodorant that covers up Eric DeCosta’s nasty work as an evaluator and negotiator and “steward” of the franchise, and they need him desperately. They need him to save the offense and therefore provide an even greater safety net to a defense that’s on fraud alert.
The Ravens especially need him to find ways to finish drives in the second half of games after Baltimore has failed to score after the half in two straight games with “genius” offensive coordinator Declan Doyle at the helm, stalling out in the redzone when they manage to get there. Jackson can’t do much to help the Ravens defensive redzone woes, but the more points the better ahead of what could be a shootout with the Bills in Buffalo on Sunday.
The Ravens rank 20th in the NFL in redzone TD% differential (-4.2%) and 25th in redzone scoring differential (-8.3%) and no one in the media is even bringing it up because of all the other chaos and noise. But if they don’t fix it soon, this season will spiral into the abyss like last year’s and they’ll keep getting Decosta-ed (blowing second-half, double-digit leads to lose) week after week.
RedZone TD Efficiency : 62.5% (13th) 3rd-and-1/4th-and-1 Rush Conv : 25% (27th)
Total Pass EPA/Game : 0.50 (14th) Total Run EPA/G : -.27 (21st)
The issues with the offensive line are getting compounded as the field compresses and the play book constricts, and as the rookie play caller gets into clutch situations in the second half of games. Doyle spoke about wanting to script even more of the game as he explained his self-scout this week; um, yeah I am not sure thinking you can have even more of the game called a day before it starts is the answer, but whatever.
“I would say I probably haven't stuck to that second-half script enough,”’ Doyle offered this week, “and I probably have to stick with my guns a little more at times, and that would be kind of my own self-evaluation of that.”
I would say Jackson is the only thing keeping this from being a bottom-eight offense, and you’d best defer to his true genius in the redzone and let him do what he wants and follow what he sees. Stay out of the way. And lean into him doing what he wants at the line of scrimmage.
The best offensive lineman on the team – rookie Vega Ioane – is out with a knee injury it will be yet another new offensive line combination (the sixth unique one to start a game). Doyle also needs to change his play calling trends now that Snoop Huntley is making way for Jackson. The Ravens are throwing the ball just 39% of the time in the RZ – 30th in the NFL – and with tight end Mark Andrews fully cooked and this team’s only big-play threat quite small to go real damage in the redzone (Zay Flowers) Doyle better start flooding this area with his rookie tight ends.
The short-yardage game with Derrick Henry (who looks like a 32-year old back and needs help in the backfield by the deadline ) hasn’t been good for over a year now, this line stinks inside (paying a ridiculous ransom of a struggling offensive lineman will go down as another DeCosta FAIL , and Doyle better lean into the option game and RPOs in this part of the field.
RedZone TD Efficiency: 66.7% (T-20th) Opposing Passer Rating : 111.7 (25th)
Pressure Rate: 30% (20th) Third Down Conv: 46.3% (T-20th)
Total Pass D EPA: -1.61 (23rd)                                 T otal Rush D EPA : -0.84 (29th)
Rookie head coach in Jesse Minter, no former head coaches on staff ( just the way DeCosta designed it ), trying to manage a defense through an entire game and run a sideline and coach an entire team for the first time on an alleged Super Bowl contender, was a big ask. Of course it’s manifesting more profoundly in the second half of games as injuries mount and adjustments are demanded in all three phases. And of course that nativity shows up most in special situations: RZ is everything in this modern game (with defensive coordinator often willing to bleed out yards between the 20s playing soft zone – and that’s all Minter does).
His defensive backs are a tragedy right now, they don’t seem connected or comfortable with his zone assignments and longtime head coach Marvin Lewis pointed out on “The Daily Flock” the obvious communication issues and bad fits in key moments. Minter best get that fixed first.
“It just starts with us putting them in a better position,” Minter said Monday. “Always starts with the coaching, in my opinion, and I'll leave it at that."
As always, we have suggestions (and they read everything, trust me).
Start with what Wink Martindale, the guy who created this defense with some help from Minter and Seahawks Super Bowl winning coach Mike McDonald, who agreed with me that Minter “needs to blitz more.” Let’s start there. DeCosta’s secondary lacks anything close to a play maker on the back end (Kyle Hamilton is a linebacker).
He also needs to get Marlon Humphrey into the slot in these tight-field situations, he should have him blitzing more from the slot and getting Roquan Smith off the field in some of these dime looks – yeah I get it he wears the green dot – is something I called for way back in the summer when defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver guaranteed an impact season.
This chart would say otherwise .
The sooner DeCosta’s made men start seeing more of the bench , the better the chances of actually keeping this from being another total disaster.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Four Storylines For Ravens' Matchup vs. Bills
full_text:
After a massively disappointing performance at home last week, the Baltimore Ravens will be back on the road in Week 8 for their third straight game against an AFC opponent with a winning record when they take on the Buffalo Bills on Sunday afternoon at Highmark Stadium.
Coming off an embarrassing loss to the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 7, in which they blew another double-digit lead after a first-half shutout, the Ravens currently have the worst record in the AFC North at 4-3 and are deservedly alone in last place.
There are several intriguing storylines surrounding this matchup between these two teams with first-year head coaches and Super Bowl aspirations. Here are the top four.
Following his first full week of practice in a month since he suffered a high ankle sprain that caused him to miss the last three games, the two-time MVP will be making his long-awaited return to the starting lineup just in time for arguably the Ravens' toughest test to date. He was a full participant all three days and was removed from the final injury report without a game designation .
"I'm always excited when I'm able to be back on the field with my guys, man," Jackson said. "[I want to] put us in the win column [and] help us get another dub. That's what I'm ready to do."
In Jackson's absence, the offense fell into a godawful rut, failing to score a single point in the second half of three of the team's last four games. The deep passing game was essentially nonexistent without him, and the ground game suffered as well, since opposing defenses didn't respect their ability to push the ball downfield and consistently loaded the box as a result.
"The sense of urgency is extremely high," Jackson said. "The divisional game didn't go the way we wanted to last week, [but] guys [have] just been hitting the ground running. [We are] just trying to get back to where we should be [in] all phases; special teams, defense and offense."
Having Jackson back, who is unquestionably the heart and soul of the team, will give them a much-needed jolt and a sorely missed confidence boost that their odds of winning are high because he's available. Nevertheless, they can't continue to be a team that only plays well in all three phases when things are going their way and can't pick themselves back up or find a way to stop the bleeding when adversity strikes.
After their other highly compensated core leaders on both sides of the ball failed miserably in their duties when it came to uplifting the team with their words and play on the field last week as the Bengals stormed back, they'll be under a microscope in this game. They need to show that they can bring their own energy and retake momentum if they get punched in the mouth instead of laying back and getting pummeled into submission over and over again, as was the case a week ago.
"We can't let the things dictate how we're going to play," left tackle Ronnie Stanley said. "We can't let things that we can't control affect us and not being a momentum-based team. We have to be able to rise above all that and play to our own standards and as if we just do this because this is what we believe, more than because people are watching or worried about the perception."
The Ravens have been held to under 100 rushing yards in back-to-back games for the first time in two seasons. Having their star dual-threat signal caller back under center will help lighten the box because of his ability to attack opposing defenses through the air with his arm and present another dangerous running element with his legs.
However, just not having their No. 1 quarterback wasn't the only reason they've struggled mightily to move the ball on the ground with any consistency or explosiveness over the past two weeks. If they want to get five-time Pro Bowl running back Derrick Henry rolling again going up against a Bills run defense that he has averaged 146.3 yards and scored four touchdowns against since joining the Ravens, they'll need to block better along the offensive line and on the perimeter for him to get to the second and third levels.
Henry has been getting contacted in the backfield and at the line of scrimmage for negative plays and minimal gains far too often. With first-round starting right guard Vega Ioane out with a knee injury in this game, they'll need their struggling remaining guards to stop up and stop blowing so many blocks, as well as better blocking execution from their tight ends.
"There are too many times where we have unblocked players that are unaccounted for that should be accounted for in the scheme," offensive coordinator Declan Doyle said. "We have to clean that up as a staff, as players, to be able to go out and execute really what looks good on paper, but we don't play the game on paper. So, as things change, pressures show up and things like that, we have to be able to echo the calls that handle those problems."
Last week, the Ravens went from making Cincinnati's Joe Burrow look rattled and playing at a less-than-pedestrian level in the first half to having a near-flawless performance over the final two quarters. He led five straight touchdown-scoring drives and threw for more touchdowns than he had incompletions, with a 4-2 ratio. Keeping Buffalo's bulldozing behemoth, that is, Josh Allen, will be an even taller task this week because of how dangerous a threat he presents with his strong arm as well as his legs on scrambles and designed runs.
The Bills don't have an advantage when it comes to talent at the skill positions, and if the Ravens' interior defensive line plays up to its potential, the two teams are pretty much equally matched in the trenches. This means this game may ultimately come down to how well they can limit Allen as a runner and improvisational passer on extended and broken plays because he's especially lethal on plays where he buys time for his running backs to leak out of the backfield and pass catchers to uncover deep downfield.
"[It] takes all 11," defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver said. "We've got to stop the run, first and foremost, [and] try not to give them [any] 50/50 run [or] pass situations. We know any time it is a pass that can turn into a run too with Josh [Allen]. [It's a] tremendous challenge [with a] tremendous quarterback. We know he's an elite [player], so it's going to take all of us."
Josh is a writer for Baltimore Ravens On SI focusing primarily on original content and reporting. He provides analysis, breakdowns, profiles, and reports on important news and transactions from and about the Ravens. His professional resume as a sports reporter includes covering local events, teams, and athletes in his hometown of Anchorage, Alaska for Anchorage Daily News. His coverage on the Ravens and other NFL teams has been featured on Heavy.com/sports, Maryland Sports Blog and most recently Baltimore Beatdown from 2021 until 2025.

title: Ravens Need To Do Some Soul Searching Ahead Of Critical Make-Or-Break Slate
full_text:
There's no denying that Lamar Jackson is the heart and soul of the Baltimore Ravens' offense and team as a whole, and fellow future Hall of Famer, Derrick Henry, admitted to as much when he spoke to the media on Wednesday.
The two-time league MVP has missed the Ravens' last three games since suffering what he later personally revealed was a high ankle sprain in Week 4.
"He's the leader of this offense, so anytime he's out there, it's always great," Henry said. "I know he wants to be out there with us and to put us in the best position to win. He wants the guys to play great as well. So, I'll be excited whenever he's back out there, and I look forward to it."
After rallying to notch a come-from-behind victory over the Atlanta Falcons in primetime in their first game without him, they went from sitting atop the AFC North standings to falling all the way to the bottom after dropping back-to-back games to the Cleveland Browns and Cincinnati Bengals over the past two weeks.
Despite being without arguably the best player in the league when healthy, they built early double-digit leads and shut out both of their rivals, only to get shut out and get outscored by 10-plus points in the second half of each deflating loss.
This past Sunday's lopsided 35-13 loss to the Bengals was equally discouraging and infuriating because of how well they played on both sides of the ball in the first half compared to the second. The lack of leadership and juice without Jackson was on full display as they put up little-to-no resistance as Joe Burrow and Co. came storming from behind to beat them on their own home turf.
It marked the second year in a row that they allowed this particular opponent to come into M&T Bank Stadium and notch a statement win by multiple scores instead of getting sent home packing.
All signs are pointing towards Jackson being available for the Ravens ' massive AFC showdown coming up this Sunday on the road against the Buffalo Bills after he's been a full participant in practice for the first time in nearly a month.
However, they are a setback away (normally a 4-6 week injury), a wrong plant or big hit away from being right back where they've been the past three weeks, looking to avoid letting history repeat itself and keep their hopes of returning to the playoffs alive without their best player.
Every team with a franchise quarterback, especially one as generationally gifted as Jackson, should be able to rely on him to give them a chance to emerge victorious whenever he's out on the field, but they shouldn't be so overdependent on him that they can't find ways to close out games without him.
The Ravens' offense has sputtered in Jackson's absence outside of promising and potent opening scripts. That shouldn't have any bearing on how the defense performs from one half to the next when it comes to maintaining focus, communication and executing proper technique, all of which waned far too many high-leverage moments in the second half over the past two weeks.
Some of these epic collapses would by no means be excusable. Still, they could be somewhat understandable for a team littered with and heavily relying on a young core of ascending playmakers who lack a plethora of big-game experience. That isn't and hasn't been the case for the Ravens since Jackson was still on his rookie deal.
The majority of the players who are responsible for the recurring mistakes that blow leads and make them a hard watch without him are his fellow established starters with years of experience and a number of impressive accolades under their belt.
"I think there's a level of accountability, especially when you're creating your own standard and culture and things like that, you have to be able to hold those guys accountable," head coach Jesse Minter said Monday.
"At the same time, normally the really good ones are the first ones coming in and saying, 'That's my fault. This was me. How do I do this better?' And so, we have a bunch of guys that take accountability when they mess something up, just like we have a coaching staff that does the same thing."
With Jackson set to be back in action against the Bills, there's no refuting that his return will provide them with a "big boost," but they can't continue to be a momentum team that constantly needs to be energized by a singular player or a turning of the tide in a game.
"We all know how good of a player he is, but we also don't want to rely on him having to carry us as a team," left tackle Ronnie Stanley said. Whoever's in there, we're confident that they're going to be able to perform, and we still feel like we had enough to win all the games that we had without him, but without a doubt, him being back would definitely be a boost."
The Ravens will face a pair of AFC powerhouses who are both currently leading their respective divisions and are legit Super Bowl contenders in back-to-back games in less than five days. After traveling to upstate New York to take on Josh Allen the Bills on Sunday afternoon, they'll turn around and host Trevor Lawrence and the Jacksonville Jaguars in primetime on Thursday night.
This team remains strong on paper and appears to be getting healthier at the right time , but they have to look inward at the kind of team they want to be and what kind of product they want to put on the field moving forward. Their fragile mental fortitude, as a result of past trauma, has continued to be the root cause of their downfall, and that needs to change.
"It's okay for players to have scars and coaches to have scars," Minter said. "I have my own scars from other places that I've been, and things like that. But it's also us collectively together, let's look at what we've been through together. Let's keep chasing how we fix ourselves in those moments.
"We've proven a couple times that we can do well in those moments, and we've proven a couple times that we haven't had what it took to close out those really tight games. Let's keep attacking it together. Let's keep adjusting our process and finding a better way for us to play well in those big moments. That's what we'll constantly be searching for."
A huge talking point around the Ravens' building in both the locker room and in meeting rooms has been the leadership, or rather, lack thereof, from prominent players aside from Jackson, especially with how lifeless the team looked on the sidelines during the second half of the Bengals' losses as their rivals rallied past them.
"I can speak for myself. I pride myself in being one of the leaders on this team," Henry said. "I am one of the vets, and I haven't been doing a good enough job as far as leading.
"When I talked about it being flat on the sidelines, when we don't have energy or things are not going the way they're supposed to, somebody has to bring that spark, whether it's speaking or out there on the field making a play that turns everything around. That's what I need to do. The leaders have to lead, have to have accountability and have to bring the juice."
Stanley shared that some of the leaders met after the game without Minter suggesting or even having to tell them to address how they can improve in that vital aspect of the game.
"Just seeing the energy that we had on the sideline when things aren't going our way is something that needs to change," Stanley said. "A lot of people have different ways they lead and different leadership styles, but I think being more vocal is something that I can get better at personally."
Following Thursday's practice, three-time All Pro safety Kyle Hamilton, one of the Ravens' most outspoken leaders, admitted that the players and coaches come together to have some "grown-man conversations" and feels confident they can get things turnaround.
"This season can go one of two different directions, and there's obviously the direction that we want to go in, so I think everybody took steps this week to give us our best chance to do that," Hamilton said.
Josh is a writer for Baltimore Ravens On…

title: Top 3 Reasons The Bills Could Expose The Ravens In Week 8
full_text:
The Ravens are getting back their franchise savior for Sunday’s game, with Lamar Jackson back from nearly a month out with a high-ankle sprain.
Jackson says the pain is “bearable” and rookie head coach Jesse Minter – who claimed for nearly three weeks this was a day-to-day-situation – is pushing the idea, hard, that Jackson will be all-systems-go and able to run as much as ever. We’ll see about all of that, but with Baltimore’s season on the brink, and it’s roster and leadership and failing general manager all in question, and with the Bills coming off the bye, this will be quite the challenge.
In situations like these, teams that do have a backbone and accountability tend to rise up and play their best ball of the season and make a statement. And that’s what will be required for the Ravens’ stumbling defense, which has not been any good for years and which is where a bulk of GM’s Eric DeCosta’s nastiest work has left even Minter – hailed as a schematic genius – utterly clueless and unmasked in the second half of games.
Getting DeCosta-ed 17 times since 2019 is no joke, and they’re managed to do it (blow double-digit leads to lose) two weeks in a row in critical AFC games. They’ve done it under two head coaches and seven coordinators but just one front office. Hmm. So maybe we get the best of what Baltimore will ever have to offer, and that had best be the case.
Even 75% of Lamar should be enough to put up points on a Buffalo secondary that is among the worst in football and has massive holes everywhere. But can the Ravens do enough to keep Josh Allen from putting up a point or two more than Jackson? I have my reservations and in particular about these four key matchup elements :
The Ravens have yet to be tested on the ground, at all. They haven’t faced an opponent that even feigns to run the ball at all; the only one that could, the Colts in Week 1, didn’t because they had a stupid game plan and they fell desperately behind early. The Saints, Bengals, Cowboys, Titans, don’t threaten anyone, and so the Ravens being 12th in success rate (22nd in EPA) probably flatters them.
The Bills are arguably the best rushing team in the NFL with a multi-faceted attack James Cook is tops in rushing yards since the start of last season and Josh Allen is a historically significant running QB who is a TD machine on the ground. When they run from middle to the left it’s six yards a carry; $30M “closer”’ Trey Hendrickson always lines up over left tackle; good luck with that.
Longtime Ravens defensive coordinator Wink Martindale said it best on “The Daily Flock” this week – Hendrickson can’t stop the run enough to get on the field on early downs for him and is a “designated pass rusher,” no matter how much DeCosta paid him . Oh, and the Ravens most complete edge defender, Tavius Robinson, is out for the season.
Suggestion : They’d better be willing to play second-round pick Zion Young way more than they have been in this one. If Minter uses a LB like Trenton Simpson to spy Allen, I suspect it comes back to bite him in the pass game.
We have been chronicling this deficiency on a weekly basis and it could be acute Sunday. Joe Burrow has so much success shredding Nate Wiggins and Marlon Humphrey on the outside racking up 35-unanswered points Sunday he didn’t need to ping tight end Mike Gesicki in the slot much. Allen is top 5 in the NFL with a 117 rating throwing to the slow since the start of last season (18 TDs – 6 INTs) and his emerging TE Dalton Kincaid is going to be a handful for this group.
The Ravens have seen the second-fewest targets to TEs in the NFL, but allow a 132.5 rating when they are thrown to, and Kincaid is catching everything he sees this season. Khalil Shakir will tear up the Ravens smaller dime defenders if they get that match up and DJ Moore (questionable) is a two-way go is a problem and he could be back for this one too.
The free yards in the slot have been a blight on Minter’s defense and if he keeps up the same dime looks with the same personnel he will get cooked again.
Suggestion : Hamilton probably needs to do the job on the tight end and Marlon Humphrey needs to be in the slot and TJ Tampa needs to get a run on the outside. Minter better be willing to get into more man looks and blitz Allen, because he will shred this defense in the quick game just like Burrow did if he isn’t in duress. (Oh and dump Humphrey's salary by the deadline)
The Ravens have doomed themselves with their character flaws week after week. If they start slowly, and have to chase the game, with a QB who was out nearly a month, that’s not great. And even if they build a nice early lead, well, we know how that goes.
The lack of experience on this coaching staff and the lack of intensity from the highest-paid veterans on the defense is a toxic combination. Minter and defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver were falling all over themselves to talk around some of their issues – blaming the crowd was quite a touch – but there better be some tough love going on in those meeting rooms.
Getting John Harbagh run out of town for these kinds of losses and then walking all over the new guy is an ugly look. Things always seem too comfortable when the GM is buddies with certain guys and plays favorites but its time for Minter to step up and shake things up. (Martindale explains the impact it has on a coaching staff and locker room here)
Suggestion : Better be ready to bench people. Needs to get real. Their paychecks are guaranteed, but DeCosta isn’t a coach as much as he preens and pretends he is on the sidelines. Trenton Simpson for Roquan Smith, Hendrickson on a pitch count, Humphrey on his way to the bench have to be on the table, and fast, if this garbage continues. If Mark Andrews plays ahead of rookies Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas on offense it’s a sign of what an unserious, totally political operation they are running. Wake up.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: What To Expect From Lamar Jackson in Week 8: Ravens MVP QB Updates Ankle Injury
full_text:
Ravens head coach Jesse Minter confirmed on Friday that the team expects Lamar Jackson to start Sunday in Buffalo after a third-straight full day of practice and sounded hopeful that the two-time MVP will be able to utilize his legs as much as possible.
Jackson, who said the pain has subsided to a large degree, returned to practice on Wednesday, able to put in a full day of work for the first time since suffering the ankle injury.  And he has continued to do more since. Snoop Huntley had served as the backup in that stretch during which the Ravens fell to 4-3 after losing consecutive games to AFC North teams in which they blew a double-digit lead. The team’s hope is that the rest and recovery have put Jackson in a position in which he will not be compromised by the ankle injury; given how bad the offensive line has been much of this season, that’s hugely important.
“I think he’ll look like Lamar Jackson,” Minter said after Friday’s practice. “He’s just done such a good job dealing with the injury … Now he’ll be in a position to play Lamar Jackson football.”
Jackson said the pain in his ankle is “bearable” and thus he can play: “I feel like I’m no longer a statue. I’m able to move around a little better. It’s time to give it a shot.”
Jackson said swelling in the ankle last weekend, after limited practices, precluded him from playing in Week 7.
Jackson suffered the ankle injury at the end of the first half in Week 4, trying to escape a sack, when he was caught from behind and his left ankle twisted in an extreme manner. Jackson made it clear he was told it was a high-ankle sprain which he called “very, very painful” when he met the media for the first time since the injury last Friday.
The Ravens insisted on having the rookie head coach refer to it as “day-to-day,” relentlessly, even through two straight weeks of Jackson doing nothing or next-to-nothing on the practice field. That only heightened the scrutiny around the situation, leading to some suggesting perhaps he could have returned sooner (and several prominent national reporters were pushing that narrative, leaving one to wonder who they were getting that directive from, because it clearly wasn’t Jackson).
“Why would you second guess me?” Jackson said Friday. “Why would you second guess me.”
Then again not much with Jackson is normal, especially in regards to general manager Eric DeCosta. Having him on a non-exclusive franchise tag at the end of his rookie deal and making him play out that first contract; opining after Buffalo’s Josh Allen got a new deal in March of 2025 that he didn’t have much contract work of his own to tend to do. And now Jackson has reached a point with this failing front office where he will be able to act as a de-facto free agent as soon as this season ends.
It’s always weird with this sophomoric GM and the greatest thing that has happened to this franchise, arguably, ever, from a personnel standpoint (a QB this transformational at the end of the first round?). Now they need Jackson to prop up a roster with massive warts and major holes – same as ever, especially a secondary that DeCosta likes to pretend is his strength . Now Jackson has to try to right another season spiraling amid pleas from an overmatched coaching staff for someone to be a leader .
Rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle, who now sounds like he wants to script the entire game beforehand (how long before he’s back on the sidelines calling plays?), had better be willing to activate Jackson’s legs more than he has to this point; the traditional run game with Derrick Henry is a joke behind another DeCosta offensive line, and they need to attack the perimeter with speed as much as possible.
A third straight loss, with a quick turnaround against Jacksonville on Thursday, could send a season teetering on the brink right over the ledge.
“The sense of urgency is extremely high,” Jackson said of a critical game with the Bills.
“I think we’ll see a great version of Lamar,” Minter said.
He’d better. He’ll need it.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: The Case For The Ravens Being NFL Trade Deadline Sellers. And Who Should Go ASAP
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens might be three weeks away from truly pivoting to playing their youngsters and embracing the fact that the alleged Super Bowl contender carried 20 percent of its roster with rookies to open the season in the first place.
If they lose to the Bills and Jaguars in the span of a few days, and if their second-half defense continues to be historically suspect, and if their novice coaches continue to looks horribly overmatched after halftime ( they should have hired them help ), and if Jesse Minter keeps wondering why his $370M roster can’t display any heart and leadership, then it just might be that this team is a mere extension of last year's disaster, and that general manager Eric DeCosta is one of the biggest frauds in the NFL, and that Baltimore is doomed again.
This might just be a bloated, complacent roster that is the handiwork of an entitled, stubborn, egomaniacal fake smart guy (just like Mike Elias), who skirts accountability and blames others and curries favor with checked-out billionaires. Meantime John Harbaugh and Todd Monken – the men allegedly holding back DeCosta’s treasure trove of talent – compete for NFL Coach of the Year honors elsewhere.
DeCosta tends to put own self-interest ahead of the team, wanting “his guys” to make him look good for rewarding them with unnecessarily rich extensions while primo young talent leaves the building (which is why the baby-faced coach is forced to start guys, who are replacement-level talent, at best, making top-10 money at their positions).
But imagine if the Ravens had an honest broker running the team. Someone clear-eyed – not a politician obsessed with his media clippings who is constantly working to hone that image – who could see this Frankenstein roster for what it is. What would they do? Well, as longtime NFL GM Marty Hurney suggested on “The Daily Flock” several times this year and again this week, this was always going to be the final year in Baltimore for a legion of starters and key reserves, and this organization might need to shift into player-development mode soon.
“At some point if things still have not gotten right, I do think you have to make that switch and start playing more of the young guys,” Hurney told me, “and try to make that transition. Because I think that every team hits it and the Ravens do a really good job, as good as anybody of really turning it over and not having the ‘window; philosophy, because they've always drafted well and had a lot of draft choices. But right now, you kind of feel like this is a time where the young guys need to step up and it feels like there's a little bit of a transition taking place in Baltimore."
Indeed, so, wouldn’t it make sense to load up on draft picks – even very low draft picks because these are more salary dumps than football trades (again, blame DeCosta and blame a half-interested owner for not rebuilding his decaying front office when he fired Harbaugh). Getting DeCosta-ed 17 times since this guy was handed the reigns from Ozzie Newsome is a sign that even Lamar Jackson can’t overcome this mess, isn’t it?
There are some moves they could make to buy on the fringes ... but DeCosta may have created more problems already with a desperate deal for Cam Jurgens . Not sure he should be trusted to add more.
DeCosta is beyond a failure when it comes to extending his QBs contract like any half-assed GM would. So Jackson can decide if he wants to go to Miami, or whatever, and DeCosta knows it, which explains why he acted like a fool at his pre-season press conference when pressed on this topic.
But if Jackson doesn’t want to take their money, he doesn’t have to, and with an $85M cap hit the Ravens would have to move him. So there’s that. Then consider that it’s painfully obvious that Ronnie Stanley, Mark Andrews, Derrick Henry, Roquan Smith, Marlon Humphrey, Rashod Bateman and Calais Campbell are at the end here (and would be if this team had a real GM in charge). And that of their young players on rookie deals, only Tavius Robinson (on season-ending IR) and Trent Simpson would be making a case for an extension.
That’s bleak folks. But that’s DeCosta, who would rather give Humphrey the 10th most money of any corner in the NFL, than admit he did another stupid contract structure and acknowledge his obvious decline  just pay him $4M to leave.
And in terms of blue chip players on a contract extension, there’s Kyle Hamilton and Zay Flowers and Nnamdi Madubuike and that’s it. Not much.
But their culture is clearly warped - DeCosta is at the core of that - and it’s not getting better and I’d be perfectly fine with taking whatever you can get for Smith and Andrews and Bateman and Humphrey right now and embracing a future without them. Move Simpson to Smith’s spot, or Teddye Buchanan, give TJ Tampa a run for Humphrey, and they drafted two tight ends who are already better than Andrews.
Now, let's be real - no one wants those veterans. No one would give DeCosta anything for Andrews after the 2024 season and he insisted in paying him again, anyway. Oh, and the real problem is his drafts have stunk too, so the next man up at these positions could be perilous.
Sending a message to the locker room and starting to position for the future isn’t crazy. If those guys can’t lead – and Minter says he’s desperately searching for leaders – then empower your youth. I don’t think the drop-off would be significant in most cases (maybe not even going from Stanley to Carson Vinson)
They're going to need to convince Jackson why he should stay, and almost none of those veterans will be back here in 2027, whether the QB is or not.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Thursday Injury Report Includes Major News For Lamar Jackson
full_text:
The Ravens have been coy in their handling of Lamar Jackson’s ankle injury for a month now.
Since the two-time MVP suffered the injury on a sack from behind at the end of the first half in Week 4, Baltimore’s offense has fallen onto a major funk, and rookie head coach Jesse Minter has walked a verbal minefield about conveying some semblance of the extent of the injury to his paying customers – through the media – but also needing to respect the player’s reputation and make it clear this is a significant setback for him to navigate that.
Ravens public relations has a poor reputation in such matters, throwing a novice head coach into the mix has only exacerbated the messaging issues, and Minter would barely saying anything on Wednesday about his quarterback other than the team would be issuing an injury report – as mandated by the NFL – and Jackson would be listed on it in some capacity. Lesson learned, it seems (be careful who you take counsel from in The Castle, rook; they’ll hide and cower and let you take the fall).
Turns out Jackson practiced in full on Wednesday , the first time he did so since before facing the Titans on Oct. 4, and he did the same on Thursday. The longer this situation played out – it was obvious he was going to miss at least two games from the onset – it became clear that Jackson was going to have to get through a full week of full practices before being activated to return to play. He is checking those boxes now.
Kyle Hamilton, the Ravens best defensive player, returned to practice Thursday as did rookie guard Vega Ioane, who just suffered a knee inury that some reported would be multiple weeks (Minter did not close the door on him playing Sunday) and middle linebcker Roquan Smith was back on the field, too, as all did not take part in any capacity Wednesday.
Should Jackson practice fully on Friday – it’s a limited workday and barring some totally unforeseen circumstance that will be the case – it’s fair to expect he will have no injury designation on Friday’s injury report. He was ruled out on Friday on each of the first two weeks after his injury – which Jackson has described as a “very, very painful” high-ankle sprain. Last week he was listed as questionable and then the team announced on Saturday afternoon that he had been downgraded to out (which raised anew questions about their public handling of this situation all along).
While Ravens rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle was being hailed as a “genius” all summer, he was quick to point out himself on Thursday he is only seven games into calling plays and is trying to adjust his processes with one of the worst second-half offenses in the NFL. Jackson is the genius, he covers up the warts on a roster that is 7-14 without him, while wins 70% of the regular-season games he starts. And if this offense rebounds, it’s because the best player in the league returned (and if it doesn’t out late-summer prediction that Doyle is going to end up calling plays from the sidelines and trying to connect better with his players is going to look sage ).
How much Doyle is willing to lean into Jackson’s legs to boost a moribund run game will be telling; he’s already riding Derrick Henry at an historic rate for any age 32 RB in NFL history , with diminishing returns. The ability to generate explosive plays will be back – Jackson leads the NFL at 10.1 yards/attempts (no one else is above 8.8) – as backup Snoop Huntley doesn’t average even six yards per pass in his NFL career.
Henry has averaged just 3.4 yards per rush the last four weeks (35th in the NFL). Getting rookie “Joker” Adam Randall (a hybrid RB/TE/H-Back/WR ), off Injured Reserve could add wrinkled for Doyle, too. Something has to change in a major way for Baltimore in the second half and this young staff better figure it out quickly. Consider that without Jackson the Ravens have fallen to 31st in second-half scoring, dead-last in third-down conversions in that half and 29th in three-and-out percentage.
Also consider how it came to pass again that Ravens struggling general manager Eric DeCosta (better do something at the deadline, hoss )  let Jackson enter a potential walk season without a contract extension after the QB had to dangle on a non-exclusive franchise tag and demand a trade to get a fair-market deal after his rookie deal expired, which Baltimore made him play out.
The Miami Dolphins badly need a quarterback and a superstar to market the team around and an identity and they are loaded with draft capital. I’m just sayin .
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Is Ravens GM Eric DeCosta At The Core Of Their Losing Ways? Longtime Coordinator Wink Martindale Thinks So
full_text:
There’s a reason so many Ravens defensive stars from the past took to social media in the aftermath of Baltimore’s pathetic second half Sunday, allowing 35 unanswered points to the Bengals and looking like quitters in the process.
Guys like Ed Reed and Terrell Suggs seemed appalled by it all , the franchise DeCosta-ed for the 17th time since 2019 (blowing a double-digit lead in the second half in a loss), and the one constant during this entire uninspired brand of Ravens football is the general manager, Eric DeCosta, who curries favor with the billionaire boss and divides the organization and plays favorites in the locker room and creates a culture that continually produces spineless results.
Yet that billionaire chose to empower him even more than ever before when he fired John Harbaugh (needed to fire them both ), and with an overmatched novice head coach on board they keep hitting new lows. Rookie coach Jesse Minter is stuck with a legion of bad contracts DeCosta handed out all over that defense, and while there are some schematic changes he is going to have to make (as we discussed with longtime head coach Marvin Lewis here ), he’s also going have a hard time altering the psyche and heart of a football team poisoned by the guy who controls the salaries.
Longtime former Ravens defensive coordinator Wink Martindale, who has known Minter forever and was invited to Ravens practices this offseason and whom Minter helped create the defensive packages that make the hub of this 2026 Ravens defense, is aghast at what’s going on in Baltimore. He knows the role that DeCosta has played in this mess better than most, and kept it real with me on “The Daily Flock” this week.
“This isn't good enough,” Martindale said. “This is not the standard. This is not Baltimore defense.  And you know, I was there first, you know, in 2012 when we won the Super Bowl with Ray Lewis. You think Ray Lewis would put up with that [crap]? You think Ed Reed would put up with that [crap)? You think (Terrell) Suggs would put up with that [crap]? You think Haloti Ngata would put up with that [crap]? …
“You can still hold people accountable and you can still say, ‘This guy's better than this guy because of this this and this. And this guy's got to play, not because of what they get paid, you know, (but because they deserve it). They got a left tackle that's been paid a [crap] ton of money who needs to step up and be a leader, you know, with Ronnie (Stanley). And I love Ronnie, and these guys I’m talking about.
“They’re good people, but God damn it, we want to win in Baltimore. And that's where I was at the longest in my career ever in coaching. I was there for 10 years. So, like my kids who were born in Ohio think they're from Maryland because that's the longest we were in place …  And I just think that they need to step up and say, ‘Here's who we're going to be."’ Yeah. And if they don't, they're going to continue to do the [crap] they're doing.”
Martindale believes $19M corner Marlon Humphrey probably needs to move to safety or just play considerably less, though the team is short of corners despite it being one of DeCosta’s primary fetishes. He wouldn’t play overpaid $30M pass rusher Trey Hendrickson on early downs as much as Baltimore is (but DeCosta demands it with that salary!). Wink believes Minter needs to start blitzing more even though it runs counter to some of his core philosophies. (DeCosta better explore some of these cheap trade deadline options , ASAP)
He gives deep explanations for such on the show. The biggest reason for the organizations falloff, he believes is the move from longtime general manager Ozzie Newsome to DeCosta. And like so many around the NFL know, DeCosta built a reputation and career off of Newsome’s accomplishments, used it to get promoted repeatedly and ingratiated himself incredibly well with Steve Bisciotti back when he was still a minority owner in the team.
“I think the biggest impact was when it went from Ozzie to Eric,” Martindale said, noting DeCosta likes to hang on the sidelines and in the locker room and fraternize with certain players in a way Newsome never considered. And I know what (Owner) Mr. Steve Bisciotti wanted to do with Eric, but I also think it's time to for Eric to step up and win a Super Bowl because, you know, Ozzie’s last draft class (2018, when he selected Lamar Jackson) you can look at his last pick – it was (defensive lineman) Zach Sieler, who’s had three contracts down at Miami now.
“And I know their (scouting and evaluation) system and I would do the same system that they have there. But there's also times where you’ve got to come to dinner and say here's what it is, and not just keep patting yourself on the back because you get an A++ in every draft (from the media).”
Truthbombs. The show is loaded with them. Not everybody can stomach frauds.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: 4 Realistic NFL Trade Deadline Deals The Ravens Should Explore Right Now
full_text:
On the field and in the locker room. The general manager, Eric DeCosta, gets more exposed every day (now the hack PR guy can’t even announce a waiver claim correctly ), and pressure is mounting on him to do something to try to fix the latest roster mess he’s created. Problem is, he plays favorites and overpays fading veterans like Marlon Humphrey and Roquan Smith (who makes Fred Warner money and check out this chart of how pathetic his production is ). So his locker room lacks heart and leadership cuz the payroll is fat and bloated and they run all over the GM, because they know they are made men with him.
Hence business decisions while getting destroyed , 35-0, in the second half by a division rival at home.
And a rookie head coach who has been on the job for five minutes is supposed to step seven years of getting DeCosta-ed (blowing second-half, double-digit leads and losing), something DeCosta has done a record 17 times since taking over in 2019). Good luck with that. (Longtime former Ravens defensive coordinator Wink Martindale breaks down the warped dynamic far better than I ever could on “The Daily Flock” show below).
So this huckster is sweating and his hands are tied with that payroll and lack of cap space – because of all those bad contracts – but, as always we’re here to help him out. And one thing you can count on: DeCosta  and that PR hack read and watch everything we do. Two of my best customers.
So here you go DeCosta – get your head out of your hands, stop feeling sorry for yourself and go do something already for the fanbase that pays your bloated salary:
Remember him? Boy could they use a super speedy twitchy back who wins in space with pure speed and athleticism and turns nothing into something. Considering DeCosta’s garbage offensive line is undermining the ability to run under center or between the tackles – Derrick Henry’s bread and butter – and the fact that Henry is age 32 (where RBs careers expire), yet he's leading the NFL in carries ( with troubling signs), They’ve got problems.
Justice Hill is not as spry as he once was, rookie Adam Randall has been on IR since the summer and will face a tricky learning curve and played RB for one year in college. They need something right now to get in the pistol with Lamar and attack outside the tackles with explosion. Things got weird between him and DeCosta (shocker), but he only makes $1.25M with a low cap hit and if they don’t get real multiplicity in run game (Henry’s is 27th in the NFL at 3.9 yards/carry), even with Lamar they could struggle to run the ball as they’d like.
The Ravens are allowing a pass rating of 122.7 when opposing QBs throw to the slot. Their two small dime backs are getting torched in coverage and they don’t see to want to move Humphrey there (he’s probably really just a box safety at this point, anyway, as Martindale suggested). Minter needs a slot defender he can trust, and Still was very good for him with the Chargers.
Good size at 6-feet, great mobility and he’s a Terp! Of course, the winless Chargers are looking to trade old and expensive players and not good and young and cheap ones. So they have no motivation to move him, but they will be making moves.
DeCosta is not well liked around the league at all – and the stunt he pulled bailing on the Maxx Crosby, while shady as hell, was totally in character for him. Luckily for him, his longtime underling Joe Hortiz – another branch on the fruitless Ozzie Newsom family tree – is the GM there and likes doing business with him and fleeced him on the Odafe Oweh deal a year ago. DeCosta keeps making desperate moves, so maybe he’ll make his old buddy an offer he can’t refuse.
DeCosta is looking for scapegoats. He had Minter railing on second-year kicker Tyler Loop two weeks ago, while they keep pretending that Jake Moody, who has never come close to establishing himself as an NFL kicker, is some sort of competition. Stop it.
Slye has been one of the NFL’s best the last three years, he is having a great season in his walk year, he is plenty young by kicker standards and only makes about $1M for the rest of the season and then is a free agent. You wanna whine now about growing pains with a young kicker they refused to push all spring and summer long, then make it an actual upgrade.
It would sting and it would hurt after bailing out of a trade for him a few months ago. But the King Of No Rings told his fanbase he had real plans to trade for Crosby and sign Trey Hendrickson . Make a long story short – despite a $150M defense this aimless “evaluator” needs Crosby worse now then he did back in March when he was spinning this yarn about landing both edge players.
With Lamar maybe a few weeks away from exposing DeCosta once and for all and going to Miami, or wherever else he wants, they better find reasons for him to stay. It’s yet another year with no offensive line and no one to throw the ball to except Zay Flowers … Could DeCosta at least build a half-assed defense? No wonder Lamar wins them 70% of the games he starts and DeCosta’s roster is 7-14 when he doesn’t.

title: Ravens Week 7 Rookie Report: Vega Ioane Left Early With Injury
full_text:
Several members of the Baltimore Ravens' 2026 rookie class saw extended action in Sunday's 35-13 home loss to the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 7. They are in an AFC North division in which every team's record is above .500, and after falling to 4-3, they now deservedly sit at the bottom of the standings heading into next week.
Drafted and undrafted first-year players saw extensive playing time in all three phases. The only rookies who were healthy scratches were fourth-round wide receiver Elijah Sarratt and undrafted quarterback Joe Fagnano, who still suited up as an emergency No. 3 option. Fifth-round running back Adam Randall wasn't activated from short-term injured reserve in his third week of eligibility and seventh-round defensive tackle Rayshaun Benny is on the practice squad and has yet to be elevated.
Here’s an overview of how these rookies performed in their late taste of NFL regular-season action.
The first-round interior offensive lineman's return to his natural position at right guard after playing the last three games at center was short-lived and cut short due to injury. After taking a knee to his right knee while making a block downfield, he left the game following that drive and did not return. It marked the first time all season that he missed a single snap on offense, as he only played 16 of the Ravens' 67 total snaps on that side of the ball. According to a report from NFL Network's Ian Rapoport , Ioane suffered a sprained MCL, and while it's not a long-term injury, he is expected to miss time. Head coach Jesse Minter alluded to the fact that he'll likely miss this week's massive matchup against the Buffalo Bills following Wednesday's practice.
"We'll see where it's at with (Vega)," Minter said. "If there's anybody that can do something crazy and overcome things, he's got the right mentality. We'll see how that goes, and we'll put the best guy out there that gives us the best opportunity for this particular game."
Despite the Ravens losing sack leader and stout run-defending fourth-year pro Tavius Robinson to a season-ending pectoral injury, the second-rounder didn't see a sharp or even slight uptick in playing time on defense, as many expected . His 21 snaps on that side of the ball were his second-lowest of the season and fewest since he played just a dozen in Week 1. He still helped the Ravens bottle up the Bengals' rushing attack to just 73 yards on the ground with an average of just 3.7 yards per carry. Young recorded his seventh solo tackle of the season on a solo takedown of running back Chase Brown after a four-yard gain to prevent him from moving the chains on a penalty-shortened first down.
The third-rounder picked up where he left off in his return from injury last week by picking up key first-down conversions on the first two of the three receptions that he made on five targets for 25 receiving yards. All three came on third down, with the first being a juggling snag he gained control of before backpedaling out of bounds for a gain of 10 yards on the Ravens' second scoring drive. Two plays later, he came up clutch again with a nine-yard snag on third-and-medium that he had to go low to pluck before it could hit the ground. His third catch came on the final play of the third quarter with the Ravens deep in Bengals territory, and had he not had to work back to the quarterback after getting sufficient depth at the top of his route, Lane likely would've been 3-for-3 on third-down conversions as he dragged down two yards shy of the line to gain.
Since his return from the wrist injury that delayed his impact as a rookie, Ja’Kobi Lane has looked impressive, becoming a popular third-down target. The Ravens struck gold in selecting him in the third round. Any questions over drafting him too early have all but disappeared! pic.twitter.com/BykC9TTRAy
Lane nearly had a mulligan on recording his first career touchdown catch on the Ravens' last possession of the first half on a third-and-short in the low red zone. Unfortunately, backup quarterback Tyler Huntley's pass was just out of reach of the long-limbed wideout, who got nice separation from the corner guarding him on the play.
The fourth-rounder played fewer than 30 offensive snaps for the first time in his last four appearances, but it was also his first game back after missing last week with an injury. Hibner wasn't targeted as a pass catcher and was one of multiple players at the position who struggled as blockers in run blocking, either whiffing or straight-up losing block attempts. With veteran Mark Andrews struggling the Ravens need to get the young tight ends more involved.
The fifth-rounder didn't see any playing time on defense for the second straight game, as the Ravens decided to deploy second-year pro Keyon Martin at the nickel spot over him again. Rivers' 13 snaps on special teams were the second-most among rookies and 52% of the team's total.
The fifth-rounder played his fewest offensive snaps since Week 2 with 15, yet that didn't stop him from having his second-most productive outing in that phase of the game with two catches on three targets for 35 receiving yards. He picked up 16 yards on the first play from the scrimmage of the game off a play-action pass from Huntley that he caught short and rumbled for the rest. His other 19 yards came on a tight end screen that moved the offense past midfield and into Cincinnati territory late in the third quarter.
First drive, double motion with Cuevas, then a chip and release to get him wide open while the defense is busy elsewhere. Good layup for Huntley that became absent one the game script became more established. pic.twitter.com/kLqZsJ4OTn
Cuevas was Huntley's intended target on the final play of that same drive, but he collided with a Bengals defender and was knocked off course just enough for the pass to fall incomplete on a fourth-down gamble by Minter, who bypassed another short field goal that would've given the Ravens the lead back.
The #Ravens failed 4th and 1. #RavensFlock pic.twitter.com/QHHOsYILtp
The sixth-round specialist had a solid yet non-spectacular day at the office with three punts for 145 yards, including an average of 48.3 yards per punt and a long of 57, his third-longest of the season. While Eckley didn't have any touchbacks, he didn't manage to pin the Bengals back inside their own 20-yard line once either.
The undrafted free agent helped fill the void created by Robinson's season-ending injury and did a great job in the effort. Burke tied his career highs with 17 defensive snaps and 22 on special teams, first among rookies and tied for the most on the team overall. He was impressive as an edge-setter against the run with how he stacked and effortlessly shed would-be blockers, and nearly notched his second career sack on Joe Burrow, who somehow managed to throw an incomplete pass before the Maryland native could bring him all the way down with possession. Burke's Pro Football Focus grade of 78.5 was the highest among all defenders on the team and second overall to only two-time Pro Bowl wide receiver Zay Flowers, who had another monster game and earned a 90.7.
Ravens UDFA Ethan Burke Welcome back Brent urban pic.twitter.com/Xzmc5DMEZ8
Josh is a writer for Baltimore Ravens On SI focusing primarily on original content and reporting. He provides analysis, breakdowns, profiles, and reports on important news and transactions from and about the Ravens. His professional resume as a sports reporter includes covering local events, teams, and athletes in his hometown of Anchorage, Alaska for Anchorage Daily News. His coverage on the Ravens and other NFL teams has been featured on Heavy.com/sports, Maryland Sports Blog and most recently Baltimore Beatdown from 2021 until 2025.

title: Rookie Report Card: Grading Every Bills Rookie's Performance After Bye Week
full_text:
Six games and seven weeks into the 2026 NFL season, the Buffalo Bills need more production from their rookie class.
Coming out of the bye week, and returning to Western New York after two games on the West Coast, this puts the Bills in an ideal position to integrate their draft picks into the gameplan more.
For now, here's a grade for every rookie based on production and performance so far this season.
The plan for Parker was never for him to take a majority of edge rusher snaps in Year 1. With Greg Rousseau, Bradley Chubb and Michael Hoecht already in the room, Parker is a long-term bet that will hopefully pay off.
For now, the second round pick has half a sack, 16 total tackles, and a forced fumble, recording just four QB pressures on 118 snaps.
IGB has been the highlight of the rookie class to start the season. Thrust into action when Christian Benford battled a toe injury and Maxwell Hairston was benched, the Ohio State product has lived up to the scouting report of sticky man coverage skills.
His 244 defensive snaps lead the team's rookies by far, and he's already recorded seven pass breakups this season ( the most by any rookie in the NFL ).
Per PFF, Igbinosun has allowed 17 receptions on 29 targets for 211 yards and two touchdowns, while surrendering just a 58.6 reception percentage.
He's had his ups and downs, but has exceeded expectations for a rookie playing one of the most difficult positions in the sport. If he can cut down on his penalties (already six this season) that would help elevate his game even more.
Bell has only been active for two games this season, seeing three targets and recording zero receptions. I went back and watched all three of his targets, and all three were either bad balls or bad decisions by Allen trying to force it to the rookie.
The UConn product has played 69 snaps yet is still waiting for his first NFL touch in an offense that's desperate for more contribution from the WR room.
After the fourth round pick looked like he was pushing Dorian Williams for a starting role over the summer, perhaps the TCU product will see more playing time if the LBs continue to struggle.
In 74 defensive snaps, the rookie's recorded 12 tackles, one stop and a pass breakup. His coverage numbers aren't great, allowing nine receptions on 10 targets for 125 yards, but he hasn't charted a missed tackle yet this season.
Like Bell, Kilgore has appeared in just two games so far this season, recording a key pass breakup on third down against the Raiders, only to surrender a deep touchdown on the following drive by not getting enough depth on his dropback.
We'll need more than 11 defensive snaps to see if Kilgore's play will have more positive or negative swings, and he's got a great chance to show just that on Sunday with CJ Gardner-Johnson facing a one-game suspension.
Doman's everything the Bills hoped for when they drafted the Florida Gator in the seventh round.
He's currently second amongst all punters in EPA per punt above expected , ironically trailing only Matt Araiza.
He's punted just twelve times, but currently holds the franchise records in yards per punt (48.7), net yards per punt (46) and percentage of punts downed inside the 20 yard line (50%).
Three of Buffalo's rookies have yet to play a snap this season, including both offensive linemen drafted.
For Reed-Adams, it's a win that he merely made the 53 man roster as a seventh round pick.
Durant is currently on IR with a neck injury in training camp, and the Bills are probably in no rush to bring him back given the current numbers game that would come with activating him.

title: Three Bold Predictions for Buffalo Bills vs. Baltimore Ravens in Week 8
full_text:
After their Week 7 bye, the Buffalo Bills are at home to host the Baltimore Ravens . Buffalo won their previous two games before their bye, while the Ravens come into this one on a two-game losing streak.
Part of that is due to the absence of Lamar Jackson, who is dealing with a high ankle sprain. The expectation is that he will be back against the Bills, although that hasn't been confirmed . Buffalo should be prepared for a competent offense either way, especially since backup Tyler Huntley is a trusted reserve with plenty of experience.
No matter who they face, the Bills would love to send Baltimore home with a loss. That becomes far more likely if they can make good on the following three bold predictions.
DJ Moore has missed the past two games due to a shoulder injury, but he's expected to return in Week 8. The Bills can use him against the Ravens, even if Baltimore enters this game on a skid.
Despite their recent losses, the Ravens are a dangerous team and Buffalo will need to put up plenty of offense. In this bold prediction, that becomes easier thanks to the return of Moore, who hauls in a touchdown pass from Josh Allen during his return to action.
Jim Leonhard has had some hiccups during his first season as the defesnive coordinator. Buffalo enters Week 8 ranked 30th in defensive scoring , something that has kept games much closer than they should be. Leonhard has a tough task on his hands this weekend, but he had an extra week to prepare.
Bills On SI's Ralph Ventre said that communication has been the primary issue as the Bills have given up far too many plays on broken coverages. With the extra time, look for Leonhard's unit to come out looking sharp as they avoid the blown coverages and force two turnovers. Add that up, and the Ravens struggle to score 20 points for the third consecutive game.
Baltimore has been solid against the run this season, entering this game ninth in the NFL in rushing defense . That's been the norm for them as they were 10th in the league last year, and they held James Cook to just 44 yards on 13 attempts.
This year, Cook gets some revenge. With an extra week to prepare, the Bills should have some decent concepts figured out, which will allow Cook to get off to a fast start. In this final bold prediction, he asserts himself against an elite run defense and racks up 150 yards and two touchdowns.

title: Bills' Final Injury Report (Week 8): Who's In, Who's Out vs. Ravens
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills will host the Baltimore Ravens for a critical AFC matchup on November 1, and they could be without up to six key players.
The Bills issued their final Week 8 injury report following Friday's practice in Orchard Park, and six of the 13 names are listed with a questionable tag for Sunday's game.
While the injury report seems a bit lengthy considering Buffalo is coming off its bye week, six of the players are already cleared for Sunday's 1 p.m. ET kickoff.
That leaves wide receiver Tyrell Shavers as the lone player officially ruled out. Working back from a torn ACL, Shavers will remain on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list for at least one more week.
Both wide receiver DJ Moore and tight end Dalton Kincaid practiced in a limited capacity for three consecutive days. They wore red non-contact jerseys throughout the week, likely more as a precaution.
Moore uncharacteristically missed back-to-back games prior to the bye week as a result of reaggravating his AC joint sprain in Week 4. The 29-year-old WR1 seems eager to return.
"The two weeks [out], it was pretty sad. I was mad at myself," said Moore on Wednesday. "Somebody put out a post on X where I was standing there watching the guys practice, that was the hardest thing about the two weeks."
Meanwhile, Kincaid banged up his ribs area during the October 18 win over the Las Vegas Raiders last time out. After being evaluated in the locker room, he returned for the remaining 8:01 on the fourth-quarter clock.
“Feeling good. Just how football goes. Some weeks will be worse than others, and then some weeks will feel great. But lucky and grateful enough to be able to go out there and practice," said Kincaid after Wednesday's practice (h/t WGR's Sal Capaccio ).
Starting right tackle Spencer Brown and primary slot cornerback Dee Alford are both questionable to face the Ravens after little practice participation this past week .
Brown was sidelined on Wednesday and Thursday before logging limited participation on Friday. Following a limited practice on Wednesday, Alford ended the week with back-to-back absences.
Forced out in Week 5 after only 16 snaps due to a back flare-up, Brown returned for the entirety of the Week 6 win in Las Vegas.
"Just lingering stuff from what's happened to me last couple weeks. What happened in that LA game, just kind of got nicked up. Took enough drugs to sedate a small elephant when I was in LA," said Brown on Wednesday. "Just took care of the body the best way I knew how and got through the Vegas game and played pretty well. Got on the bye week, kind of bit me in the butt a little bit."
Brown, who has a history of back issues, appears to be a true game time decision. Should Brown be unavailable, expect Tylan Grable to start.
Meanwhile, it seems as if Alford could have tweaked his previously-injured ankle during Wednesday's practice. The defensive back initially suffered the injury against the New England Patriots in Week 4.
Alford sat out the Week 5 game in Los Angeles, and he returned to his regular role in Week 6 against the Raiders, seeing 43 snaps.
With the downward participation trend as a sign, Alford appears headed toward a game day inactive.
In a positive development, outside linebacker Bradley Chubb ditched the red non-contact jersey on Friday. He was a full participant on Friday, and the Bills did not give him a designation for Sunday.
Defensive linemen Ed Oliver and TJ Sanders are also good to go in Week 8. Oliver missed the past two games due to a knee injury.
Also along the defensive front, outside lineback TJ Parker is questionable with a knee, although he did improve to full participation on Friday. Defensive tackle Greg Gaines tweaked a csalf during practice, and he's questionable as a result.

title: Five Key Things to Know About Bills vs. Ravens in Week 8
full_text:
It was a pretty good Week 7 for the head coach Joe Brady and the Buffalo Bills .
While the AFC East frontrunners were getting some extra rest, the rival New England Patriots were taking it on the chinstrap at Soldier Field on a Thursday night in the form of a 30-24 loss to the Chicago Bears.
After seven weeks of action, Brady’s team is tied for the best record in the conference with the Kansas City Chiefs at 5-1. Meanwhile, the reigning AFC champions sit at 4-3 and have already lost as many games as they did in 2025. However, keep in mind that Mike Vrabel’s team handed the Bills their lone loss of the season, a 29-26 setback in Week 4 at Highmark Stadium.
Speaking of 4-3 teams, the Baltimore Ravens are currently bringing up the rear in the AFC North. The team has dropped two straight and comes off a 35-13 home loss to the Cincinnati Bengals. The club has missed quarterback Lamar Jackson, who is expected to return this week after missing the team’s last three games. That means another possible classic clash between the two-time NFL MVP (2019 and 2023) and Bills’ quarterback Josh Allen—who won the award in 2024.
Ravens vs Bills Week 1, 2025. pic.twitter.com/D1x5Rrtm30
These clubs will clash for the eighth time in nine seasons, and that includes playoff clashes in 2020 (17-3) and 2024 (27-25)—both Buffalo victories at home. All told, the clubs have split 14 overall meetings (7-7) dating back to 1999. A year ago on a Sunday night at Orchard Park, Buffalo trailed 40-25 with less than 12 minutes to play before Allen and company rallied for 16 unanswered points and a 41-40 triumph.
In Baltimore’s four wins this season, running back Derrick Henry has totaled 451 yards from scrimmage and scored seven TDs, with Baltimore totaling 24-plus points in each victory. In three losses, Henry has been limited to just 196 scrimmage yards and one touchdown and the Ravens have totaled 40 points.
There’s been plenty of entertaining football when Joe Brady’s team has taken the field. The league’s highest-scoring team (32.8 points per game) has is also allowing the third-most points per contest (28.5). The AFC East leaders have scored 33-plus points and allowed 30 or points in four of their six games.
Jesse Minter’s team owns a 4-3 record and a mere plus-2 scoring differential (169-167). It’s been a tale of two halves for the Ravens. Baltimore has outscored the opposition a combined 118-53 in the first 30 minutes. In the second half and overtime, Minter’s squad has been more than doubled up, 114-51.
Josh Allen’s first start in this series came in 2019—a 24-17 home loss. He threw for 146 yards and one touchdown, was sacked six times and lost a fumble. In the last five meetings (including playoffs), Allen has thrown for 1,120 yards (4 scores), run for five TDs, and committed two turnovers. And the Bills are 4-1.
