title: Packers Midseason Stock Report: Risers and Fallers After 5-3 Start
full_text:
Just like that, we’re at the halfway point of the Green Bay Packers’ 2026 season. They are 5-3 and positioned to make a run at another playoff berth, if not more.
Not everything has been perfect. All three of their losses have come against NFC opponents, and two of which have come against divisional foes. They’ll get a chance to bounce back against Minnesota and Detroit at Lambeau Field later this season.
They have gotten contributions from a wide range of players, and some have seen their value to the team rise during the course of the year. Others have taken a step back. With half a season in the books, who are some guys that are rising and falling? We analyze that here.
Some eyebrows were raised this offseason when the Packers gave Christian Watson a lucrative contract extension to keep him in Green Bay for the foreseeable future. Watson has always carried value in Green Bay’s offense even if he did not have the gaudy box score numbers to show for it.
This year, he has found the box score numbers to match. He is on pace to not just top 1,000 yards for the first time in his career; he’s on pace to reach 1,500 yards. He has grown into a leader in the receiver room, as well, with that leadership on display Thursday night as he was willing to play through significant pain.
Watson’s toughness and ability to fight through a broken rib impressed all of his teammates, and showed why everyone in the organization raves about him whenever they get an opportunity.
Through eight games, Watson leads the team in yards and touchdowns. He has 16 fewer targets than Matthew Golden, but is just one catch behind him. Watson is ascending into a star, which is exactly what Green Bay’s passing game needs him to be.
It’s OK to admit it. You wanted Jim Leonhard, the former Wisconsin Badgers player and coach, to be the team’s defensive coordinator after flirting with the job in the past.
It’s OK to admit that you watched the clips from HBO’s Hard Knocks and were worried that Jonathan Gannon was a strange guy who could not possibly motivate a defense after failing as a head coach.
It’s also OK to admit at this point that if you thought that, you were wrong. Gannon’s defense has been excellent for most of the season. They gave up 39 points in the first game of the year at Minnesota and 35 against Atlanta two weeks later.
Those two performances are really skewing what has otherwise been a really strong showing from Gannon and his defense early in the season.
He has not had his best player for the entirety of the season with Micah Parsons still not practicing. His next-best player, Edgerrin Cooper, played 14 quarters before bowing out with a torn Achilles.
What has Gannon done? He has weaponized his defensive backs and moved them all over the formation.
Gannon’s defense is much more aggressive than any of the men who have preceded him during the Matt LaFleur era. He’s not a loud, boisterous personality like Rex Ryan. He’s not outspoken like some other great defensive coordinators have been.
What he is, is a darn good coach.
The Packers rank fourth in defensive DVOA. They are third in yards allowed per play, including fourth in passing yards allowed per play.
He’s also got collective buy-in from his players. One of the marks of a well-coached team is when the players in the locker room are all saying the same things as the coaches and their fellow players. Green Bay’s defense is constantly repeating the same lines that Gannon states to the media. They’re parroting terminology from each other, as well.
Gannon’s defense looks fast, disciplined and confident in everything it’s doing.
Soon, it will get Parsons back, too.
“I can’t say enough great things about our defense, Jonathan Gannon,” LaFleur said after Thursday’s game. “The job he’s done, just being aggressive the entire game and putting a lot of pressure on the quarterback.”
The potential bad news here is that if Gannon keeps this up, he may get another opportunity to be a head coach somewhere else.
Yes, Golden has had some issues with drops. In fact, he leads the league in drops. You know how you get to the point where you lead the league in drops? You’re always open. Golden is almost always open, and leads the team in receptions with 43 in his second season. He’s second to Watson in touchdowns with four.
Watson and Golden look poised to be the first pair of Packer teammates to break 1,000 yards receiving in the same year since Jordy Nelson and Randall Cobb did that in 2014.
Yes, Golden needs to clean up the drops. He knows that, but he certainly looks the part. If he keeps getting open, the ball will come his way. If the ball keeps coming his way, there’s a good chance he’s going to keep making plays as he has all season.
The Packers are relying on Jordan Love more than they ever have during his time as the starting quarterback.
When Love took over for Aaron Rodgers in 2023, the idea was to keep a team around him that made it so he did not have to play the role of Superman every week. Through eight weeks this season, it’s hard to tell where the Packers might be if Love was not playing as well as he did.
Thursday’s game against Carolina might be a perfect microcosm of the Packers as a team. Love started out the game on fire, completing 17 of his first 20 passes with two touchdowns to get the Packers out to an early lead.
He threw a third touchdown pass in the third quarter to make the score 27-10 and it looked like the Packers were going to coast to victory.
From there, the lack of running game bit the Packers as Love cooled off. He threw a bad interception on a pass he said he wished he had back right after the game ended.
As Love cooled off, the Panthers crept closer. Ultimately, Green Bay was able to escape with a 27-19 victory, but it never should have gotten that close.
Love is operating with an offensive line that has gotten him killed almost every week. His run game is nonexistent. His receivers lead the league in drops. His team leads the league in penalties.
All the while, Love has continued to play as well as he ever has. He’s thrown 16 touchdown passes to just six interceptions. He might work his way into MVP conversations if the Packers can continue to win with him playing well.
Perhaps the two biggest beneficiaries of Jonathan Gannon’s defense coming to Green Bay have been the defensive backfield duo of Evan Williams and Javon Bullard.
Bullard is the team’s nickel defender. He has a tenacity that has been missing from this Packers defense for years. He hunts opposing ball-carriers, and has been asked to hunt opposing quarterbacks more than ever.
“Yes. Not even close,” Bullard said when asked if he was blitzing more this year than last year. “The trust that the coaches have in me, I’m so grateful for that. We come to practice, we work every day, we put things on tape that coaches notice. Some coaches have the guts to dial them. up, some coaches don’t. You respect the ones that do.”
Bullard does not have a bunch of gaudy stats in the box score, but his fingerprints are all over the game whenever Green Bay’s defense is on the field.
Evan Williams has been one of the beneficiaries of Bullard’s willingness to do the dirty work. He does have the box score numbers to match the impact he has made, as well.
Along with the team lead in tackles, Williams has two interceptions, one sack, six PBUs, two tackles for losses and one fumble recovery. Gannon’s willingness to deploy his best defensive players all over the formation makes them unpredictable and more disruptive than they were in recent years.
As a result, the Packers have surpassed their number of takeaways from 2025. Bullard and Williams are big reasons for that.
Far and away the worst part of Green Bay’s team is its run game. Words like historic and generational are often thrown around too loosely, but if you can think of a bad superlative, it fits this Packers team.
The Packers are on pace to break records in a bad way for how putrid they’ve been on the ground…

title: Three Overreactions From Packers’ Win Over Panthers: This Will Ruin Season
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers beat the Carolina Panthers 27-19 on Thursday night. It wasn’t pretty and it wasn’t easy – these Packers are incapable of such things – but a win is a win, and they have five of them in eight games.
Here are our three big takeaways.
Jordan Love’s numbers are mediocre.
His level of play, however, has been worthy of MVP consideration.
Of 29 qualifying quarterbacks, Love is smack dab in the middle with a passer rating of 92.5. He is 22nd in completion percentage. Only five quarterbacks have thrown more interceptions.
But Love has had to carry a heavier load than perhaps any quarterback leading a playoff-caliber team. The pass protection hasn’t been good enough, though it was against Carolina. No quarterback has been saddled with a worse running game. No quarterback has had to overcome more dropped passes or a higher percentage of dropped passes.
Love is not going to win MVP; Buffalo’s Josh Allen, who probably has fewer passing-game targets than Love but at least has a really good running game and reliable pass protection, is in his own tier as the strong favorite at FanDuel Sportsbook .
NFL MVP typically goes to the quarterback with great numbers on a great team. Love won’t finish with great numbers and the Packers aren’t a great team. But they would be absolutely sunk without him. If that’s not valuable, what is?
As coach Matt LaFleur said after a game in which Love threw three touchdown passes: “Can’t say enough great things about him because he’s carrying the burden of everything right now.”
Before the season, I predicted the Packers would finish with an 8-9 record. The reasoning was rather simple. How could the Packers without Micah Parsons find a way to stop quality quarterbacks with an ineffective pass rush and questionable cornerbacks?
It appears I’m going to be “flying the L” on that one because defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon has turned lemons into lemonade.
Parsons, one of the NFL’s best pass rushers and defensive players, still hasn’t returned to practice. The team’s next-best defensive player, linebacker Edgerrin Cooper, suffered a torn Achilles in Week 4 against Tampa Bay.
And yet, the Packers emerged from Thursday’s game ranked 11th with 20.5 points allowed per game. They are third in yards allowed per play, fourth in yards allowed per passing play and 12th in yards allowed per rushing attempt. Their 15 takeaways through eight games are one more than they had all of last season. They’ve allowed 20 or fewer points in five consecutive games, their best stretch since 2022.
And it’s not as if it’s Xavier McKinney snagging interceptions left and right or Lukas Van Ness has played up to Parsons’ hype. Six players have at least one interception. Five players have forced at least one fumble. Six players against Carolina had one sack, meaning 11 have at least one this season.
At cornerback, Keisean Nixon is thriving in Gannon’s system and rookie cornerback Brandon Cisse is playing beyond his years.  The rookie class of Cisse, defensive tackle Chris McClellan and edge Dani Dennis-Sutton are playing a lot of snaps and all made big plays against Carolina.
With the expectation that Parsons will return to practice next week , a defense that has done more than survive without its All-Pro could really start to thrive for the stretch run.
A couple weeks ago, the Packers faced the Cowboys, who had the worst run defense in the league at the time. Green Bay managed 57 rushing yards with a 2.2-yard average. On Thursday, the Packers faced the Panthers, who took over as the worst run defense in the NFL. The Packers rushed for 66 yards with a 2.5-yard average.
The running game is a disaster. It’s no longer a matter of a small sample size of games or a bad game or two to skew the numbers. The Packers are averaging 60.6 rushing yards per game, which would be the worst in NFL history, and 2.85 yards per carry.
The Packers have 485 rushing yards in eight games. Ten individuals have more rushing yards through six or seven games. Somehow, they’ve gone from bad to worse, with a 2.58-yard average the last three games.
Their best rushing game was 86 yards at Tampa Bay, which leads to this incredible stat from The AP’s Josh Dubow:
The 5-3 Packers are 5th team since 1933 to rush for fewer than 90 yards in each of the first 8 games of a season. Others: 1990 Colts 2-6 1941 Rams 2-6 1940 Eagles 0-8 1935 Pittsburgh Pirates 3-5
Somehow, the Packers are 5-3 despite a running game in which the old “3 yards and a cloud of dust” mantra would be a huge win.
Fewest yards rushing/game for team with winning record thru 8 games of a season: 2026 Packers (5-3) 60.6 2016 Giants (5-3) 68.3 2009 Chargers (5-3) 69.6 2007 Packers (7-1) 72.1 2016 Vikings (5-3) 72.6
Green Bay’s running game, in a word, stinks.
The Packers have had six starting combinations on the offensive line and 11 individuals have started a game. Nothing – nothing! – has mattered. Every team has had at least two 100-yard rushing performances and the league median is four. Green Bay hasn’t even reached 90 yards.
The Packers ran the ball 26 times against the Panthers. Against the worst run defense in the NFL, half of them gained 1 yard or worse. The longest of Josh Jacobs’ 21 carries gained 6 yards.
Green Bay won the game but was fortunate to do so. And here’s where this season will eventually be crushed.
At some point, you have to be able to go into your 4-minute offense and run for two or three first downs to win the game. The Packers were in that situation twice vs. Carolina. On the first, they took over with 5:37 on the clock. Every play on the possession was a pass. On the second, Jacobs rushed for 5 yards and 3 yards to set up Jordan Love’s third-down conversion to Christian Watson. However, Jacobs ran for minus-3, 0 and 1 on the next three plays to give the Panthers the smallest glimmer of hope.
If the Packers can’t run the football successfully against the worst run defenses in the NFL, how are they going to be able to run the football against the best defenses?
Packers are averaging 60.6 yards rushing/game and 2.85 yards/carry. That's lowest per carry thru 8 games since 2016 Vikings at 2.71 and lowest per game since 2019 Bengals were at 59.5 The only team in last 80 seasons to be that low in both thru 8 games was Washington in 1961…
Seattle and San Francisco, two teams who could be standing in Green Bay’s way in the playoffs, rank second and third in yards allowed per carry. Houston and Buffalo, who loom on the late-season schedule, are eighth and ninth. Next week’s opponent, New England, is 11th.
Eight games into the season, there seemingly is no hope.
Don’t take my word for it. Here’s what Matt LaFleur said after the game:
“If I’m being honest, not a lot right now, and that’s our job as coaches. We got to figure it out, because it’s not good enough.”
LaFleur and the coaches had all offseason to figure it out. All of training camp and the preseason to get it started. Eight regular-season games to get things pointed in the right direction.
Jacobs is back in the lineup. Veteran blockers have been signed. New line combinations have been tried, including bat-bleep loony ones such as moving Laken Tomlinson from left guard to right guard – a position he hadn’t played since 2016 and hadn’t practiced since joining the Packers.
Nothing has worked. Not even a little bit. Somehow, it’s actually gotten worse.
“I think that’s an area we’ve got to keep getting better at, keep finding what’s working, but we’ve got to improve because, especially late in the game, you’ve got to be able to lean on that,” quarterback Jordan Love said. “Obviously, late in the game, it wasn’t good enough. We weren’t able to finish the way we wanted so that’s something we’ve got to improve on, clean up as an offense and be better there.”
Love’s exactly right. Knowing there’s a problem and actually fixing it, of course, are completely different things.
In 2021, it seemed obvious all along that the special…

title: Snaps, Studs and Duds: Analysis From Packers’ Win Over Panthers
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers won for the fourth time in five games on Thursday night, beating the Carolina Panthers 27-19.
Green Bay’s defense has held five consecutive opponents to 20 points or less, a first for the team since 2022. With two more takeaways added to the tally, the Packers are up to 15 – one more than last year’s full-season tally.
Here is our weekly analysis of the Packers’ snap counts along with a few studs and duds.
Green Bay played 69 snaps on offense.
Quarterback: For the seventh time in eight games, Jordan Love played every snap. According to Pro Football Focus, he was pressured on 13 of 41 dropbacks. By the official stats, he was neither sacked nor hit.
He was excellent, save for the late interception, which he said would “haunt” him. He finished 30-of-41 passing for 288 yards with three touchdowns.
Running backs: It’s back to old times for Josh Jacobs from a workload perspective. He played 49 snaps, or 71 percent. The other 20 snaps were almost equally divided between MarShawn Lloyd (11) and Pierre Strong (nine). Kaleb Johnson was inactive.
Of the team’s 26 running plays, Jacobs got 21 of them. He averaged just 1.9 yards per carry with a long run of 6. Of his 39 rushing yards, we gave him 37 after contact. Added together, Jacobs got 27 touches for a meager 52 yards, though he did score two touchdowns.
Receivers: Matthew Golden was questionable with a shoulder injury but wound up playing a unit-high 59 snaps. Savion Williams was next with 38. Christian Watson played 34 snaps despite being hospitalized briefly with a broken rib. J. Michael Sturdivant played a season-high 29 snaps, four more than Bo Melton.
Watson caught eight passes for 113 yards. He had 100 yards before the injury and a big third-down conversion late in the game. Golden caught 7-of-13 targets for 79 yards. He had two drops for a league-worst nine; he wasted no time in making amends for the second drop by scoring a 24-yard touchdown on the next play.
Williams was a nonfactor in the passing game, but his 18-yard sprint on an end-around led by Tucker Kraft and Anthony Belton was the team’s only run longer than 6 yards. Sturdivant got one opportunity and made a terrific all-hands over the middle for a gain of 16.
Tight ends: Tucker Kraft played a season-high 61 snaps. That’s a huge workload, even for him, but necessitated by Jonnu Smith being a healthy scratch and Josh Whyle dropping out with a concussion after three snaps. Mark Redman played 27.
Kraft caught six passes for 53 yards and one touchdown; he would have finished with 74 yards if not for an ineligible-man-downfield penalty that wiped out an excellent screen.
Offensive line: The latest rendition of the offensive line consisted of left tackle Jordan Morgan, left guard Aaron Banks, center John Williams, right guard Laken Tomlinson and right tackle Anthony Belton. They played every snap.
Banks was back in the lineup after five games on the sideline due to knee and toe injuries, with Tomlinson moving over to right guard, where he hadn’t played since 2016 and didn’t get a real week of practice to prepare.
PACKERS WIN!! Thank you 2016 Laken 🫡 🙏🏾 #gopackgo #trenchwarfare #TNFonPrime
“Just when you look at it, the way Laken’s been playing, you can’t take him out of the lineup, and I thought Aaron Banks coming back, we went that route,” coach Matt LaFleur explained. “That’s not to take anything away from (Kevin) Zeitler. We feel good about him as well. But we thought that was the move.”
Williams got the nod at center following last week’s injuries to Sean Rhyan and Jacob Monk.
. @Panthers @packers @John_Williams_ first start for John Williams ; pretty good stuff for a 7th rounder out of @GoBearcatsFB #gopackgo #BaldysBreakdowns pic.twitter.com/jXDj4Ckhou
PFF charged the line with nine pressures – four for Williams, four for Banks and one for Tomlinson, with the tackles pitching shutouts. The run blocking, well, you know how that went.
Green Bay played 73 snaps on defense.
Defensive tackles: It was business as usual with relatively equal playing time. Karl Brooks led the way with 49 snaps. Devonte Wyatt, who had a huge sack on the opening drive to hold the Panthers to a field goal, was next with 40. Rookie Chris McClellan, who had a big fourth-down stop to start the second half, played 27 snaps. Anthony Campbell was next with 25 and Jordon Riley, playing in his second game in less than a week following last year’s torn Achilles, went from 29 to 19.
McClellan was in on six tackles. Everyone else on the unit combined for three (two for Wyatt, one for Campbell). Campbell and Brooks had two pressures apiece.
Edges: It was a typically balanced approach here, too. Lukas Van Ness led the way with 46 snaps. He was followed by Brenton Cox with 38, Barryn Sorrell with 33 and Dani Dennis-Sutton with 32.
All four players had a sack. According to PFF, Cox had a team-high six pressures, followed by Dennis-Sutton with five and Van Ness with four. Next Gen Stats produced similar results, with six for Cox, five for Dennis-Sutton and five for Van Ness.
Arron Mosby played 19 snaps on special teams in what will be his last roster elevation of the season. The next time the Packers want him on the field, it will be as a member of the 53.
Linebackers: With Zaire Franklin inactive for a second consecutive game, Isaiah McDuffie played every snap and Ty’Ron Hopper played 70. They usually are two vital cogs on special teams, so there’s been some adjustment with Hopper playing eight snaps and McDuffie only three.
Hopper was one of the big stars of the show with eight tackles, one sack, two quarterback hits, one interception and three passes defensed. He became the team’s first linebacker since 2000 with one sack, one interception and at least three passes defensed in a game.
Unprompted, coach Matt LaFleur said: “Ty’Ron Hopper, I can’t say enough great things about him, the night he had. What a great performance.”
Nick Niemann, who played one snap on defense, logged a team-high 22 on special teams. Kristian Welch played 19 on special teams.
Cornerbacks: Keisean Nixon and Brandon Cisse both played 72-of-73 snaps. They did a tremendous job in limiting quarterback Bryce Young and premier receiver Tetairoa McMillan.
According to PFF, Cisse broke up more passes (two) than he allowed completions (one) and Keisean Nixon, who was questionable with a shoulder injury, wasn’t even targeted. Next Gen charged Nixon with two catches for 27 yards and Cisse with one for 11. Whatever, they were excellent.
Carrington Valentine played two snaps and Kamal Hadden played one.
Safeties: Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams played every snap and Javon Bullard was on the field for the 57 snaps of nickel.
Williams had 10 tackles. McKinney had only three, but he had a big third-down breakup that preceded Chris McClellan’s fourth-down stop. Bullard, playing in his 40th game, still doesn’t have an interception but at least he finally has a forced fumble, which came on the lateral play at the end of the game.
Kitan Oladapo played one snap on defense and 18 on special teams.
WR Christian Watson (duh): Watson caught six passes for 100 yards in the first 21 minutes before being hospitalized with a broken rib after a 53-yard catch. Straight out of the WWE, Watson returned from the hospital and finished the game.
“I see Christian running out and he was just resurrected,” Jordan Love said.
He had a big third-down conversion in the final moments.
“Honestly, right when we were finally leaving the hospital,” Watson said of when he knew he could return to the game. “He was like, ‘Everything checked out.’ He asked me, ‘Are you good to still go out there?’ Before I even left, I wanted to go back out there, so I was going to make sure I was going to get back out there if they let me.”
Packers pass blocking: Jordan Love enjoyed his best protection of the season, though it certainly helped that the Panthers were playing without their best pass rusher. From a clean pocket, Love…

title: Packers Report Card: Big Win Over Panthers Comes With Two F’s
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The grades are in, and they are all over the map. The Green Bay Packers looked like they were going to cruise to victory when they took a 27-10 lead in the third quarter against the Carolina Panthers on Thursday night.
As has been the case in Green Bay for most of the season, nothing can be easy. The Packers continue to find ways to make things interesting. A Jordan Love interception gave the Panthers some life. The lack of run game gave the Panthers some hope.
Ultimately, Jonathan Gannon’s crew suffocated the Panthers’ offense in the biggest spots of the game, allowing the Packers to escape Lambeau Field with a 5-3 record.
Jordan Love had one major blemish on the night. His interception early in the fourth quarter took away the chance for the Packers to kick a field goal for what would likely have been an insurmountable 30-13 lead. Had he led Matthew Golden on the play, or seen a wide-open Christian Watson on the other side of the formation, the Packers may have had an even bigger night offensively.
“That’s really the play that is going to haunt me from that game,” Love said. “We had a concept with mirrored goes on the outside. I wanted to take a shot to MG and I saw him go inside on the route and just really a bad decision by me. I left it way inside and the safety was able to come over and make an interception that was really easy.
“In that situation, third down, in field-goal range, I’m really sick about that decision. That’s where I got to be better so we can put a team away and be able to go up multiple scores.”
Before that? He was excellent. He completed 17 of his first 20 passes and all three incompletions could have been called drops.
Watson’s toughness was on full display . He had 100 yards before going to the hospital after suffering a broken rib and coughing up blood, then returned and made a key third-down conversion late in the game.
What a night for Christian Watson. He had 100 yards before he was injured, wound up in the hospital for testing, and then made a key catch late in the game. How did he do it, and why? @JacobWestendorf explains both. ⬇️ https://t.co/aLlVfB2TSX
Love’s 30 completions went to seven different receivers, including a touchdown apiece of Tucker Kraft, Matthew Golden and Josh Jacobs.
Do the Packers need to figure out a way to ask their quarterback to not be superman every night? Yes. Can they rest assured knowing they have a chance in any game they play because of the way Love plays on a weekly basis? Also yes.
The offensive line stinks, though it at least didn’t give up a sack. The receivers lead the league in drops, with two more for Golden giving him a league-worst nine. The run game is nonexistent. None of it matters. Love continues to play high-level football. If they can eliminate some of the mistakes, the offense can reach new heights.
Everything felt like it was in line for a big night for the Packers’ ground game. Or at least something resembling a breakout.
Josh Jacobs was back for his second game and facing the worst rushing defense in football. Instead, the Packers finished with 66 rushing yards and a 2.5-yard average. The only real burst came on a reverse to Savion Williams, which picked up 18 yards. The traditional run game managed 50 yards on 25 carries.
Jacobs wound up with 39 yards on 21 carries. In the first half, he carried 10 times for 14 yards with a long rush of 4. He did create a touchdown essentially on his own when he danced around a would-be tackler at the goal line for a touchdown that gave the Packers a 13-10 lead in the first half.
Jacobs may still be shaking off some rust after missing six weeks of action, but his return has not fixed all that ails them on the ground. The Packers cannot simply rely on their passing game to move the ball as the games get more important.
The Packers became the first team in NFL history to have a winning record through eight games despite having fewer than 500 rushing yards.
“I think that’s an area we’ve got to keep getting better at,” quarterback Jordan Love said. “Keep finding what’s working, but we’ve got to improve because, especially late in the game, you’ve got to be able to lean on that. We did some really good things and I think, obviously, late in the game, it wasn’t good enough. We weren’t able to finish the way we wanted so that’s something we’ve got to improve on, clean up as an offense and be better there.”
If they cannot move the ball on the ground against Dallas or Carolina, the two worst rush defenses in football, it’s fair to ask if they ever will.
The Packers’ pass rush came back to life against Bryce Young and Co. Panthers left tackle Rasheed Walker did not have the revenge game he was hoping for in his return to Lambeau Field as the Packers piled up six sacks from six different players and pressured Young on nearly half of his dropbacks.
Brenton Cox, Dani Dennis-Sutton and Lukas Van Ness combined for 16 pressures. Along with Barryn Sorrell, all four edge players had a sack. Devonte Wyatt had a big one to kill the Panthers’ opening drive, which began at the Packers’ 29 following a fumbled kickoff return.
Young was only able to muster 209 passing yards on 41 pass attempts. That gets knocked down to 176 net passing yards with the sacks.
The Packers’ pass rush has been inconsistent for most of the season, but they have proven themselves to be good at defending opposing passing games.
That’s true despite missing some premier players on the defensive side of the ball. Their fourth preferred linebacker, Ty’Ron Hopper, started in place of Zaire Franklin and had a huge night. He blasted Bryce Young early in the game, chased Young down for a sack, had an impressive pass breakup and was rewarded with an interception after Lukas Van Ness got into his face for pressure.
The only blemish was a 26-yard touchdown to Jalen Coker in which Evan Williams and Keisean Nixon missed tackles on his way to the end zone.
Other than that? It was a big night. Now, Parsons perhaps is set to return to the practice field as the Packers face the biggest test of their schedule starting next week in Foxborough against the New England Patriots.
Chuba Hubbard was the focal point of Carolina’s attack but managed only 81 yards on 22 carries. Green Bay continues to slow down opposing ground games to earn the right to rush the passer.
When they earned the right, they unleashed hell on Bryce Young. The Panthers’ ground game is no slouch, and the Packers were in control most of the night against Hubbard.
Outside of one really bad game against Atlanta’s Bijan Robinson, this group in general has been excellent all season. The Packers have been a mirage before in terms of stopping the run. They’ll be tested in the near future, and as the calendar turns to December with Buffalo and Chicago on their schedule in particular.
If they can continue to slow down opposing ground games when Parsons returns, that will make defense more fun for Jonathan Gannon to call.
It was not exactly a banner night at the office for the Packers’ special teams.
The first quarter alone featured Coleman Owen fumbling on the opening kickoff return, which Carolina recovered and turned into a field goal. Following a touchdown pass from Jordan Love, Trey Smack had a pair of errors, starting with a league-leading eighth missed kick and his third missed extra point of the season.
Smack followed that up with a kick into the end zone for a touchback, gift wrapping the ball to the Panthers at the 35. That drive ended in a touchdown to give the Panthers a 10-6 lead.
Smack received a couple of Bronx cheers from the almost-77,000 fans as he made his other two extra-point attempts in the first half. That’s the situation the Packers’ kicking situation finds itself in at midseason.
If you want any sort of glimpse into how everyone is feeling about the kicking situation in Green Bay, Matt LaFleur told you everything you needed to know.
A long field goal would have given the Packers a 30-19 lead that…

title: After Six-Sack Game, Packers’ Matt LaFleur Has Perfect Six-Letter Word for Jonathan Gannon
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Carolina Panthers entered Thursday night’s game at the Green Bay Packers ranked fifth in total offense and sixth in scoring. Quarterback Bryce Young, running back Chuba Hubbard and receiver Tetairoa McMillan gave them a quality trio of playmakers.
But not against Jonathan Gannon.
The Packers beat the Panthers 27-19 at Lambeau Field. Gannon’s defense was instrumental, highlighted by six sacks coming from six individuals.
“Yeah, that’s great. It was great,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “It was just the relentless pressure. I thought our guys did a great job up front. I think some of the looks that we’re giving them, the opposition, Carolina, are very difficult. We do a lot of different things off of it. So, I think that’s a big-time credit to our defensive staff.”
Then came the money line about Gannon, who he hired in the offseason.
“JG, he likes to use this word a lot. I think he’s a savant. But he does a great job putting those guys in position. But it doesn’t mean anything if they can’t go execute it. So, just the ability for our guys – we’ve got a lot of smart players out there – to go out and be able to do all that, that’s a big-time credit to our players.”
Gannon on a short week put together a game plan that limited the Panthers to two touchdowns, 258 yards, 3.7 yards per play and 5-of-18 on third down.
“I think every time we get to third down, we just trying to get off the field,” Xavier McKinney said. “Even in the huddle, we like, ‘Ay, we need to get off the field right here.’ I thought the play calling was good. Especially on third downs, I thought it was really good. I thought we were pretty much in the right call every time.
“And guys went out there executed. The rush was getting there, so didn’t have a whole bunch of time, so just collectively everybody did what they were supposed to do.”
Young, who the Packers spoke highly of all week, was 23-of-41 passing for 209 yards. McMillan, who ranked in the top 15 in catches and receptions even while playing one fewer game than most receivers, caught only 6-of-11 targets for 58 yards. Young’s 26-yard touchdown pass to Jalen Coker late in the game was the only reception of 20-plus yards allowed.
Young was just 1-of-6 on passes thrown 10-plus yards downfield.
“They executed better,” Young said. “A lot of that stuff was on film, but they do a really good job of disguising. They are a good defense, and we have a lot of respect for them. They were better than us today for sure. They deserved that win. We should have been better. You have to execute better. That’s all it is.”
The mistake-plagued Packers did their best to help keep things interesting. Coleman Owen fumbled the opening kickoff return, handing the Panthers the ball at Green Bay’s 29, but Gannon’s defense held them to only a field goal following Devonte Wyatt’s third-down sack. Early in the second quarter, Christian Watson fumbled, giving the ball to the Panthers at their 37, but they went three-and-out.
That was one of four consecutive series in which they failed to pick up a first down and gained a total of 10 yards.
“I feel like that’s the hallmark of a good defense,” safety Evan Williams said. “You got to be ready at any time. Can’t rely on anybody to help you out. It’s a plus, it’s a cherry on top if the offense is doing their thing and going hard, but our standard is keep them out of field-goal range, keep them out of that half of the field, as a whole. You got to be ready for anything in this league. Anything can happen at any time. I feel like guys responded well.”
Williams and Isaiah McDuffie had 10 tackles apiece and Wyatt, linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper and edge players Lukas Van Ness, Barryn Sorrell, Dani Dennis-Sutton and Brenton Cox all had sacks.
Hopper stole the show. Making his second start for injured team captain Zaire Franklin, Hopper piled up eight tackles, one interception and three passes defensed. He was the first Packers defender since Charles Woodson in 2009 with at least one sack, one interception and three PBUs in a game.
After the Packers took a 13-10 lead in the second quarter, Hopper deflected and intercepted Young to set up a touchdown that extended the lead to 20-10.
“I was just able to get my hands up,” Hopper said. “We knew he was a shorter guy, so they talked about getting your hands up throughout the week. And I was able to do that and get my hands on the ball.”
After the Panthers pulled within 27-19 with 5:37 remaining in the game, Green Bay’s offense had a feeble three-and-out that took barely 1 minute off the clock.
Carolina, which had trailed by 17 points early in the third quarter, suddenly had a shot to at least take the game to overtime. Instead, Gannon’s defense thwarted four consecutive plays, including a six-man pressure on fourth-and-5 that forced Young’s errant pass to McMillan, who was covered by Javon Bullard.
“I think we did our job,” Bullard said. “You know, it ain't always gonna be perfect. We definitely got some things we need to clean up but, at the same time, walked out of here with a ‘W’ against a good team, and that's always our goal at the end of the night. You know, it ain't going to always be pretty, but you get a job done. That's all that matters.”
The Packers produced two takeaways; they’ve had at least two in five consecutive games. Their 15 takeaways through eight games are one more than they had all of last season.
While the defense was making big plays, it wasn’t allowing any. Entering the game, Carolina was seventh with 23 completions of 20-plus yards. The Packers, as noted above, allowed one.
“I just like the aggressive style,” LaFleur said. “They put a lot of pressure on offenses. We knew going into this, I think Carolina led the league in most explosive passes in the league, and they just didn’t allow that to even kind of happen.”

title: Here’s Why Packers WR Christian Watson Returned from Broken Rib
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Green Bay Packers receiver Christian Watson had just made a 53-yard catch to put his team in position to take the lead on Thursday night against the Carolina Panthers.
There was one problem as he laid on the ground. He couldn’t breathe. Watson laid motionless on the grass at Lambeau Field, not knowing what had happened to him.
“I think I just came down on the ball or my elbow or something,” Watson said. “I couldn’t breathe on the field. I got the wind knocked out of me. I got back to the sideline and I was kind of spitting up some blood or something like that.”
Watson revealed that he had a broken rib that presumably was going to knock him out of the rest of the game. Watson was taken to a hospital for precautionary reasons, despite his objections.
“So, the doctor said I had to go get a CT. I was trying to beg them to not make me do that, but it is what it is,” Watson said. “Thankfully, I was able to get the CT, everything looked good. I got a rib, that’s all. The major stuff was all good. No internal bleeding or anything like that, so I was able to get back out there. That was an experience, for sure.”
Football is a game in which violence is glorified. Players run into each other for a living. Playing with pain is an expectation.
That’s especially true in the Watson family, where all three men have played at the professional level. Watson grew up with an older brother and father who would chide him into getting up as soon as he was laying on the field. That was a rule in the Watson household. Playing through pain once you’re standing? That’s the expectation, as well.
“We would always kind of chirp at each other if you know anyone was laying on the ground too long,” Watson said. “We just always had the mentality to get up, anyway. So, yeah, if you can get up, you have to get up.”
With Watson headed to the hospital, the assumption was that he would miss the rest of the game, considering the situation was similar to the one that he faced last year in Denver. Ultimately, Watson injured his shoulder and did not miss any time last year.
One hour after being unable to breathe, Watson returned to Lambeau Field in a scene that was straight out of WWE. The only thing missing was entry music for The Undertaker with the way Watson re-entered the game.
“Yeah, it was pretty remarkable,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “He was coughing up blood, and so they took him for precautionary reasons and had to check him out. Obviously, he cleared that, and the grit to go back in the game, he had a heck of a night. I can’t imagine what he would have had (statistically) had he not missed so much time.”
Watson’s night was off to an excellent start when he left the game. In about 21 minutes, he had eclipsed 100 receiving yards and was asserting himself as the best player on the field, his fumble notwithstanding.
When he returned to the stadium, the Packers were leading 27-10. Why did he return to the field?
Simply put, that’s the expectation.
“Honestly, I feel like before I even left, I wanted to get back out there,” he said. “This means everything to me, to be out there on the football field. Like I said, I’ve had injuries that I was not able to go back out on the field after for, and I missed a significant amount of time with injuries.
“So, any chance I get to go out there on the football field, I’m going to be out there on the football field. everyone’s hurting somewhere. Everybody is feeling something. Just got to fight through it and keep on going.”
Watson finished the night with eight catches for 113 yards. His final catch was a big third-and-2 conversion in the fourth quarter.
Watson had rotten injury luck earlier in his career with soft-tissue injuries along with the ACL injury he suffered in the season finale of 2024. The question with Watson has never been ability, but whether his body would allow him to showcase his obvious talent.
Through eight games, Watson is well on pace to shatter his career highs in receptions, yards and touchdowns. According to the team, he is the first Packers player with 40-plus catches, 700-plus receiving yards, six-plus receiving touchdown and an average of at least 16.5 yards per catch in the first eight games since Jordy Nelson in 2013.
He is Green Bay’s best receiver on the field, but also sets the standard off of it.
His football character is sky high. His teammates rave about him. He’s blossomed into a leader of his position group.
When the game ended, his teammates were both in awe, but not surprised that Watson returned to the lineup in order to play through pain.
“I think it’s incredible. I think it shows resiliency, I think it shows toughness and I think it just shows the love that he has for this team,” safety Xavier McKinney said. “Sometimes, you might see that happen and he had his 100 yards and he could’ve just sat it.
“But the fact that he wasn’t satisfied and the fact that he felt like and he knew that we still needed him out there and he still said, OK, I love this team and I want to be able to go out here for this team and do that, that gains our respect. We respect him for that and sh**, we love him for that, we appreciate him for that.”
What about his quarterback? What did Jordan Love think about his top receiver returning to the lineup?
“That just speaks and is a testament to who he is and what type of player he is,” Love said after the game. “But not only that, what kind of will he has because, man, that’s crazy. A lot of people would never, especially a receiver, but for him to come in and keep playing and then still make plays, I mean that’s huge.”

title: Packers’ Josh Jacobs Clarifies Viral Touchdown Celebration vs. Panthers
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – After the first of two touchdowns against the Panthers on Thursday night, Green Bay Packers running back reacted with what seemed like a provocative celebration in which his hands were behind his back.
The Amazon Prime Video cameras didn’t show the “whole celebration,” Jacobs said after the game.
Packers RB Josh Jacobs, who was arrested on misdemeanor battery in May, pretended that he was being handcuffed after his touchdown run. (🎥: Amazon Prime Video) pic.twitter.com/kUJEnLsXpM
“Sh**, it was f***ing 1 second that they just showed me,” Jacobs said after a 27-19 victory in his second game back with the team after spending six weeks on the exempt list for an incident with a woman.
“But, anyways, me and Savion (Williams) came up with a celebration – if they would’ve seen the whole celebration. Basically, last week, we said the first celebration when I score, I was going to thank God; that’s what I did last week. The second one was going to be “ Break Every Chain .” It’s a gospel song, that was going to be the next celebration. It’s just a correlation, but like I said, the media [is] going to run with it. They’re going to make it something that it wasn’t, but it is what it is.”
The cameras only showed Jacobs with his hands behind his back as if he’d just been handcuffed.
“That wasn’t the whole celebration. It was more to it than that,” Jacobs said. “They stopped showing the celebration after that. So, like I said, it is what it is.”
Jacobs has not saved the running game . It was the worst in the league without him and it’s been the worst in the league with him.
Against a Carolina defense that entered Week 8 ranked last in the NFL in rushing yards allowed per game and per carry, Green Bay’s abysmal running game managed just 66 yards on 26 carries – a feeble 2.5-yard average.
Williams had a game-high 18-yard run. Otherwise, Jacobs mustered just 39 yards on 21 carries – a woeful 1.9-yard average – with a long run of 6.
“I felt pretty good with what I could do,” Jacobs said. “I tried to make the plays when they was there. It wasn't a lot out there, but I tried to make the plays when they was there.”
He made a couple of key plays. On third-and-goal at the 1 midway through the second quarter, he used a jump cut to get him into space for an easy touchdown run that put the Packers ahead to stay at 13-10.
Then, midway through the third quarter, the Packers faced a third-and-1 at the 4. Jacobs was wide open for an easy touchdown catch from Jordan Love.
Jordan Love (17) to Josh Jacobs (3) Green Bay Packers 4 yards pic.twitter.com/e68Q3B4c1J
Those touchdowns were part of the Packers going a season-best 3-of-3 in the red zone.
“Just the dynamic player that he is in the pass game and the run game, it’s amazing to have him back out there,” Love said. “It’s two games in for him – he missed a lot of games – so he’s going to keep getting rolling.
“We talk about it, you look at the stats, our run game isn’t where it needs to be, but he had two touchdowns tonight. Just looking at that, that’s what he’s capable of and that’s what he helps bring to the offense. We’ll keep leaning on him, keep finding ways to get him the rock, but he’s a dynamic player. He does it in the pass and the run game. So, it’s great to have him back.”
The hope is Jacobs will get better as he gets into a groove and the line will get better once it gels. It’s possible the guard combo the Packers rolled out on Thursday for the first time, with Aaron Banks back in the lineup at left guard and Laken Tomlinson flipping to right guard, will have some staying power to help get things cranked up.
“It’s a lot of turnover,” Jacobs said. “Obviously, we got a lot of injuries in that (OL) room, so it’s a lot of guys trying to get a feel for each other. But I just try to make the plays when they’re there and then, when they’re not there, still try to create and get the most out of every play.
“But definitely when they’re there, I just try to make the play and it’s just something I feel like as a unit we got to be better at, just more intentional with, straining a little longer, me running a little harder. All those things correlate.”
For Jacobs, it was his first home game since the incident over Memorial Day, which wrapped up legally with him pleading no contest to misdemeanor battery and criminal damage to property. Officially, the league says the investigation is ongoing, though the reality is the league shut it down weeks ago other than waiting to see if it will get access to video of the incident.
While there are fans who no longer want Jacobs on the roster, the reaction during introductions was mostly positive.
“It was good, man. I think it was good,” Jacobs said. “I think it was good for the team. It was good to be out there – Thursday night, electric, stadium packed. As an offense, we had our little lull moments but the defense held it down in this game.”
Asked what it meant personally, Jacobs mostly focused on the Packers winning the game and improving to 5-3.
“Oh, yeah, definitely a lot, man,” he said. “Being able to go out there and make some plays, still a lot to clean up, still a lot to work on, but it’s still positive. We’ll never apologize for winning.”

title: Packers Winners and Losers: Christian Watson Goes From Ambulance to Starring vs. Panthers
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers needed to bounce back against the Carolina Panthers after Sunday’s loss to the Detroit Lions. A win would keep them within striking distance in the NFC North. A loss would put them at risk of falling four games behind the Minnesota Vikings in the loss column.
As has become the norm for this year’s version of the Packers, sloppy football followed. They lost two fumbles and missed an extra point in the first half alone. Jordan Love’s red-hot start, however, allowed the Packers to take a 10-point lead into halftime.
The second half started with Jordan Love throwing a touchdown pass to Josh Jacobs to give the Packers a 27-10 lead that despite some of their best efforts, they would not relinquish.
He was excellent most of the night, and leads off our weekly list of winners and losers.
How good was Jordan Love in the first half? Well, he started 17-of-20 passing. All three of his incompletions were on dropped passes by Matthew Golden and Christian Watson. Maybe you could argue Watson’s drop was a pass breakup, but the point stands. He was dealing in the first half. That performance comes behind a bad offensive line and a run game that cannot find any traction no matter the opponent.
The Packers know better than anybody what can happen when asking a quarterback to carry the entire ship.
Usually, that ship sinks because quarterbacks, like everyone else, are human. The evidence came in the second half as Love threw an interception on the second play of the fourth quarter to give the Panthers some life.
Matthew Golden on 2nd down: Drops a TD Matthew Golden on 3rd down: Catches a TD. Jordan Love didn't hesitate going back to him. 💯 pic.twitter.com/eJwpUEg1kB
Apart from that critical mistake, the second half was much of the same for Green Bay’s offense. Love continued to dice apart a Panthers defense that was missing some of its stars. The first drive of the second half finished with a four-yard touchdown pass to Josh Jacobs to give the Packers a 27-10 lead.
Love finished the night 281 yards on 40 pass attempts, three touchdowns and one interception. The entire offense, as it has for most of the season, fell on him.
He looked like he was in total control of the offense most of the night. Nothing seems to faze him, no matter what happens during the game.
Yes, they were playing a Carolina defense that was decimated, but those are the teams that great quarterbacks light up.
Love lit up the Panthers in prime time and was the single biggest reason his team got to 5-3.
In what looked straight out of a WWE script, Christian Watson left the game in an ambulance in the first half, and returned with just over four minutes to play in the third quarter.
Yes, you read that right. Watson laid motionless on the Lambeau Field grass after catching a 53-yard bomb and you could hear a pin drop in the stadium.
Christian Watson is back!! 🚨 What a moment. (via @packers ) pic.twitter.com/xOv1db19bQ
As everyone feared the worst, Watson had to leave the stadium in an ambulance for precautionary testing.
The official announcement was a chest injury, and it felt like a near certainty he’d miss the rest of the game if not more.
Instead, Watson returned to the game in the third quarter. Playing hurt in the NFL is an expectation, not an exception. Still, the toughness is admirable.
Oh, and on the field before he left the game, he was the Packers’ best receiver. He’d caught six passes for 100 yards before leaving the game in an ambulance.
His final catch of the game also helped the Packers pick up a critical first down to essentially run out the clock and avoid disaster. Watson is someone held in high regard by his teammates, and Thursday's game was a big reason why.
In a season full of next men up, Ty’Ron Hopper became the latest one last week after a freak injury to Zaire Franklin came to light in practice. Hopper replaced him and played solid in his debut as the Packers’ new linebacker next to Isaiah McDuffie.
Hopper had a huge first half against Carolina. On the second series of the game, Hopper was sent on a pressure and decked Bryce Young on a vicious hit that forced an incompletion and a punt.
Later in the game he was locked up in coverage on Chuba Hubbard before forcing an incompletion as Young threw the ball down the field. His biggest play was a case of being in the right place at the right time.
Lukas Van Ness batted a pass from Bryce Young into the air that fell into the waiting arms of Hopper with the Packers leading 13-10 in the second quarter.
He added a sack in the second half by chasing down Bryce Young.
Hopper is going to need to play well for the team with Edgerrin Cooper out for the season and Franklin having an unclear return date.
If he keeps making the plays he made in the first half on Thursday, the Packers may keep him on the field when Franklin returns.
Through the first month of Zeitler’s tenure in Green Bay, it made sense that Zeitler would not be ready to play due to sitting on the couch for most of the offseason.
The sense of that decision ended on Sunday in Detroit. It made less sense on Thursday against the Carolina Panthers.
Travis Glover, the person who has been starting at right guard since Zeitler signed in Green Bay, was inactive with a knee injury.
It felt like Zeitler was set to make his debut as the starting right guard. That was not to be. Aaron Banks was active, and took his place at left guard.
The starting right guard was someone who had 13,920 fewer snaps than him at right guard. Those snaps all came in 2026. Laken Tomlinson took the starting role.
Zeitler was paid real money to save Green Bay’s offensive line after a disastrous performance at the end of September against Atlanta.
He was likely under the impression he was going to play when he was ready. Zeitler has said he’s ready to play, but remains on the bench.
Nobody can seem to figure out why.
The Packers lost their one free possession of the game. How? Their new kickoff returner, Coleman Owen was hit by Jackson Kuwatch of Carolina, forcing a fumble.
Owen’s snap was his first as a kick returner. He had been returning punts and was signed to the active roster thanks to the high ankle sprain for Skyy Moore, who remains on injured reserve.
He replaced J. Michael Sturdivant in that role, who had been solid if unspectacular in Moore’s absence.
The Packers’ defense would hold the Panthers to a field goal attempt when a third down sack from Devonte Wyatt ended the Panthers’ opening series.
It’s difficult to generate explosive returns as a kickoff returner, so ball security has to be a priority.
At some point, questions need to start getting asked. Trey Smack was given virtually no competition this offseason, and quieted some questions with a perfect preseason.
Smack came into play Thursday with five missed kicks in the last three games. Last week, he cost the Packers six points in a game they lost by three.
His first attempt to kick on Thursday he hit the left upright. He followed that up by kicking the ball into the end zone, gift wrapping the Panthers great field position for the ensuing possession that ended in a touchdown.
If there were any example of how bad things have gotten for Smack, Matt LaFleur bypassed a 53-yard field goal that would have given the Packers an insurmountable lead to have Daniel Whelan pooch punt with 30 seconds left in the game. He does not trust his kicker.
Smack currently leads the league in missed kicks with eight. Five field goals and three extra points. For those that are good at math, that’s 18 points that have been left on the field this season.
The next time the Packers play, the calendar will have flipped to November. That means that the games are getting more important. The more important the game, the smaller the margin for error.
The Packers cannot afford to have their kicker lighting points on fire.
If it’s not going to happen against the Dallas Cowboys or Carolina Panthers, it’s probably not going to happen at all…

title: Christian Watson Returns from Hospital, Packers Beat Panthers
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – With 9 minutes left in the second quarter on Thursday night, Christian Watson caught one of those majestic deep passes from Jordan Love. It was a beautiful throw and a beautiful catch.
And a violent ending as Watson and cornerback Will Lee IV tumbled to the turf, with Lee falling on Watson. Both players stayed on the turf for a couple minutes before Watson – in full uniform – stepped into an ambulance to go to a hospital for testing.
The Green Bay Packers trailed the Carolina Panthers 10-6 at the time. Less than 20 minutes of game time later, with the Packers leading 27-10, Watson jogged through the stadium, ran out of the tunnel and joined his teammates on the sideline. After Carolina capped its drive with a field goal, Watson was back in the game. He was targeted on his first play back in the game and caught a short pass later in the series.
Highlighted by Love’s early destruction of the Panthers’ depleted defense, Watson’s remarkable return to the lineup and the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers soaking up the cheers and doing Lambeau Leaps during a TV timeout, Green Bay overcame a sloppy start to beat the Panthers 27-19 on Thursday night at Lambeau Field.
The Packers have won four of their last five games to improve to 5-3. The Panthers, who started the night leading the NFC South, fell to 3-4.
The Packers took a 27-10 midway through the third quarter. Along with the theatrics of Watson’s return, a blowout win seemed like a formality.
But nothing is ever for these Packers.
Trailing 27-13 and facing a fourth-and-3 with about five-and-a-half minutes left, Bryce Young hit Jalen Coker over the middle, and he dodged a couple would-be tacklers for a 26-yard touchdown. Carolina went for two but Isaiah McDuffie broke up Young’s pass, keeping the score 27-19.
The Packers then had a horrendous three-and-out. A 21-yard screen to Tucker Kraft was wiped out by an ineligible-man-downfield penalty and Love was flagged for intentional grounding on third-and-10 following a wayward shotgun snap by John Williams.
After the punt, Carolina started at its 45 with 4:35 to go. But Green Bay’s defense wouldn’t budge. Devonte Wyatt’s tackle for loss on first down set the stage for Young’s incompletion on fourth-and-5. Defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon sent six and the Panthers picked it up, but Young’s pass to Tetairoa McMillan was short of its destination.
The Packers entered the game with the worst rush offense in the NFL. The Panthers had the worst rush defense. Carolina won the matchup decisively, but it all came down to the end and whether Green Bay could run out the clock.
Jacobs gained 8 yards on two tries, setting up third-and-2 with 2:33 to go. With the game on the line, Love connected with Watson over the middle for 7 yards and the pivotal first down.
Green Bay needed one more first down to officially put the game away, but Jacobs was buried for minus-3 on first down, with the clock winding down to the 2-minute warning. His second-down run got stuffed. His third-down run was lucky to gain one. So, with 29 seconds left, coach Matt LaFleur sent out the punt team.
Dani Dennis-Sutton’s sack essentially ended the game.
Even while losing Christian Watson to a chest injury and two early fumbles, the Packers led the Panthers 20-10 at halftime.
Jordan Love was on fire against a Panthers defense playing without their two starting cornerbacks, a fill-in starting cornerback and their top pass rusher. Love ended the half 18-of-24 passing for 192 yards and two touchdowns. Two of the incompletions were drops by Matthew Golden.
Golden made amends for the second. After dropping a 24-yard touchdown pass in the right corner of the end zone, he caught a 24-yard touchdown pass to the left on the next play. That gave Green Bay its 10-point halftime lead – a remarkable feat considering Coleman Owen fumbled the opening kickoff return, Watson fumbled later, Trey Smack missed an extra point and Josh Jacobs had 14 rushing yards on 10 carries against the worst run defense in the NFL.
Carolina got the ball to start the second half and drove out to midfield. Coach Dave Canales went for it on fourth-and-2 but rookie defensive tackle Chris McClellan stuffed running back Chuba Hubbard for a turnover on downs.
The Packers wasted no time in scoring what seemed like the clinching touchdown. Jacobs got the ball six times on the drive, including a 4-yard scoring pass from Jordan Love. The play, which gave the Packers a 27-10 lead, pushed Jacobs over 10,000 scrimmage yards in his career.
Carolina won the toss and deferred. The Packers had been going with Bo Melton and J. Michael Sturdivant on kickoff returns. This time, it was Melton and Coleman Owen. Owen did a nice job fielding the bouncing kick but got blasted by linebacker Jackson Kuwatch. Owen fumbled and the Panthers recovered at Green Bay’s 29.
The defense did well to limit the damage to a field goal. After giving up one first down, Lukas Van Ness set the edge on a first-down run, Ty’Ron Hopper had great coverage on a second-down checkdown and Van Ness and Barryn Sorrell corralled Bryce Young in the pocket so Devonte Wyatt could get the sack.
After an exchange of punts, the Packers took advantage of good field position to score the go-ahead touchdown. On third-and-8, Jordan Love ripped a post to Christian Watson for a gain of 24. Then, on third-and-8, Tucker Kraft got open on a post against safety Nick Scott for a 12-yard touchdown.
Trey Smack’s extra point hit the left upright, and the rookie heard the boos as he walked off the field.
Smack’s kickoff was a touchback, giving the ball to Carolina at the 35. Bryce Young hit tight end Tommy Tremble for 19 on third-and-3 (17 yards after the catch) and Chuba Hubbrd for 11 on third-and-10 (16 yards after the catch with two missed tackles) to get the ball into scoring position.
Brewers in the house and doing Lambeau Leaps. pic.twitter.com/hZ7Eiqydkk
With the Brewers being celebrated between quarters, the crowd was going nuts on second-and-goal at the 1. Hubbard silenced them immediately with a touchdown.
Green Bay had a drive going on its ensuing possession but Watson fumbled after a third-down catch. The defense, once again, did the job. Brenton Cox and Karl Brooks had pressures to force a three-and-out punt.
The Packers then drove 90 yards for the go-ahead touchdown. The big play – and the costly play – was a 53-yard bomb to Christian Watson. It was a perfect throw and excellent catch, but Panthers cornerback Will Lee IV fell on Watson at the end of the play. Both players stayed on the turf for a couple minutes before Watson walked off the field, into the blue medical tent and then the locker room.
On the next play, Savion Williams gained 18 on an end-around; Tucker Kraft and Anthony Belton had big blocks. Finally, on third-and-goal at the 1, Josh Jacobs used a wicked jump cut to find space for an easy touchdown. The crowd roared, then roared even louder when Trey Smack made the kick to give Green Bay a 13-10 lead.
Watson had 100 receiving yards in about 21 minutes before the injury.

title: 7 Texans Trade Candidates to Watch Ahead of NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline is right around the corner; less than two weeks away.
Which means, for the Houston Texans, now becomes the perfect time to take a step back, look at this current roster, and see how this group could be tweaked or improved in order to bounce back from an ugly 2-5 start.
It also becomes time for the Texans to look at some talents on their roster and determine whether or not they should be considered long-term pieces of the puzzle. And if they aren't–– for whatever reason–– maybe putting them on the trade block could be a worthwhile decision.
And for these seven Texans players in particular, perhaps a mid-season trade could be within the best interest of both parties.
The Texans' wide receiver depth looks a whole lot different than it did at the start of the season when they traded for Kayshon Boutte , leading to a suspicion that Houston might not have him in their long-term plans after this season when factoring in his expiring deal.
Perhaps there's a case for the Texans to pivot on Boutte before even getting to the end of this season. The past two weeks have led to Boutte seeing his lowest snap totals of the season. And with guys like Marvin Harrison Jr. and Tank Dell due to eat into his snaps as an outside receiver, maybe it'd be best for Houston to punt on him now and cash in some value rather than later.
Another wideout in a similar boat as Boutte: he's in the last year of his respective contract, might not be a priority to re-sign this summer, and is in a wide receiver room where he might only continue to see his snaps taken away week by week.
The difference for Hutchinson is the fact that the Texans used him a ton within their offensive game plan last week. Between the last two weeks, Hutchinson has found his way onto the field for over 50% of Houston's offensive snaps for the week. So compared to Boutte, maybe he has a better chance of sticking around.
While the Texans had good intentions to bring in Wyatt Teller as a hopeful upgrade on their offensive line, he hasn't quite met the standard for what Houston has been looking for through the first half of the season. The only reps he's gotten as a starter since arriving is when Ed Ingram was out for two weeks thanks to a groin injury.
Maybe the Texans decide now is the right time to send Teller elsewhere. They could cash in some minor value for their offseason investment, and send out a veteran guard that might still have a chance to contribute better elsewhere.
Pretty much the exact same deal here for Smith. He was signed as hopeful starter on the Texans offensive line this offseason on his $20 million deal, but suffered a foot injury before the beginning of the season that derailed any momentum to beat out Trent Brown for his respective spot.
So maybe the Texans can go and find some value on the trade market for Smith, rather than make his $20 million investment look like a waste . And as a tackle, compared to a guard like Teller, there's a better chance that Houston's front office can strike on a bit better trade value here.
Jake Andrews is an underrated trade candidate to keep an eye on. While not the most flashy name on the offensive line, he was someone who proved to be a serviceable starter at center for Houston all throughout last year, yet saw his spot taken by Evan Brown to kick off the 2026 season, and has been left in the shadows ever since.
The return on an Andrews trade could be minimal, but maybe it helps sweeten their future pool of assets enough for the Texans' front office to ponder it.
Now, maybe the Texans don't want to send it in on David Montgomery this early. He's only played a quarter of the season with his new offense, and hasn't been able to bounce back from a poor start because of the groin injury he suffered in Week 5.
But Montgomery has certainly underperformed from where his initial expectations stood upon the Texans' trading a fourth-round pick for him. Maybe another team out there needs help in the backfield and feels that they can get a second wind out of the veteran running back that Houston hasn't been able to find. Mark this one down as unlikely, though.
Davis Mills is always going to be a name floating around in Texans trade rumors for as long as he's on the team––which is simply because of his status as a quality backup quarterback. If Houston sees a quarterback-needy team on the market, sending them a stopgap veteran like Mills could result in a nice return.
But there is a ton of value in having a strong backup being your QB1––even if that signal-caller is playing lights out like C.J. Stroud has so far this year. And when factoring in Mills' expired contract, a trade might become even more appealing.

title: Where Texans' Playoff Odds Stand at the Bye Week (There's Still Hope)
full_text:
The Houston Texans are heading into their Week 8 bye with a whole lot less optimism surrounding their chances to make the postseason compared to where things stood to start the year off.
Before the 2026 season started, many saw this Texans roster capable of not just winning the AFC South, but stacking up as one of the premier Super Bowl contenders around the NFL.
A dominant defense, a much-improved offense, and a quarterback-head coach duo that has made the playoffs each of their three seasons being paired with one another; there was lots to feel good about for this Texans unit.
However, fast forward to the middle point of the Texans' season, and things haven't quite panned out as well as they would have liked. Houston's 2-5, coming off one of their worst losses of the year against the New York Giants , and their chances of being one of the seven teams to claw into the postseason have dwindled pretty noticeably.
That's not to say their chances are totally dead in the water, though––especially knowing that this Texans team has been prone to make a late-season run just as recently as last season.
Honestly, when taking a peek at just where the Texans' playoff odds stack up after dropping five of their first seven games on the season, you might not believe that they're truly a 2-5 football team.
According to odds from FanDuel Sportsbook , the Texans are currently +200 to make the NFL playoffs, which, when stacking those chances up to the rest of the AFC, places them with the 10th-best odds within the conference to make a run to the postseason.
The only teams that the Texans rank ahead of? That's the Las Vegas Raiders (+560), Indianapolis Colts (+1500), New York Jets (+1600), LA Chargers (+3500), and a pair of teams that don't even have eligible odds to make the postseason: the Miami Dolphins and Tennessee Titans.
Of course, it's not exactly the most favorable company for the Texans to be included with. Those six teams with playoff odds below Houston have a combined record of 9-31. But there's certainly more reason to believe in a late-season run for this Houston roster than those aforementioned five.
For one, this Texans roster has more than enough talent on both sides of the ball. Houston has a total of six Pro Bowlers still onboard from last season that might've not played up to that level early on in the year––Kamari Lassiter, Azeez Al-Shaair––but has the resume to support that they can turn things around in the weeks ahead.
But on top of that, the Texans' successess in the second half of the NFL calendar have been well-documented ever since DeMeco Ryans took the reigns as head coach back in 2023.
From Week 9 onwards since 2023, Ryans has a collective record of 20-9, which reached its peak back when the Texans went on a nine-game winning streak to close out their previous 2025 campaign, and perhaps something similar could transpire in the coming weeks.
Through the next three games, Houston does have some winnable matchups on tap : a road trip to face the Chargers, a date against former Texans quarterback Deshaun Watson and the Browns, and a rematch against the Colts after their prior loss back in Week 3.
Perhaps another late-season run could be brewing for the Texans. However, there's no question that if Houston wants to make their fourth consecutive playoff berth, wins have to start piling up, and fast. Time will tell if they can.

title: Why Texans May Not Miss Jaylin Noel as Much as Expected
full_text:
The Houston Texans' latest injury to their roster is one that certainly stings.
Earlier this week, the Texans placed second-year wide receiver Jaylin Noel on injured reserve with a toe injury that's expected to sit him out for the remainder of the regular season .
Seeing any player go down with a season-ending injury is a tough pill to swallow, but that's especially so when losing out on a talent like Noel after the year he's put together. Noel has actually led Houston's offense in total receiving yards (331) and yards per reception (17.4) through their first seven games.
However, while losing Noel does take a hit to the Texans' overall offensive ceiling, it's certainly not time to panic as to how this passing attack is able to move forward.
In fact, the Texans might be able to stay afloat within their air attack pretty easily–– and that's because of the recent developments around their wide receiver position as a whole.
Sure, losing out on the explosiveness and playmaking ability that Noel provides is going to be hard to replace within the offense. He is the Texans' leading receiver on the year for a reason after all.
But the Texans' wide receiver room, which once was void of depth within the first few weeks of the regular season, has now turned a corner in a big way heading into their Week 8 bye.
That's because of the acquisition of not only Marvin Harrison Jr., who was brought in via trade after Houston's Week 5 win over the Tennessee Titans, but also the return of Tank Dell , who officially made his way back onto an NFL field for the first time in nearly two years this past weekend against the New York Giants.
Those two factoring into the mix are massive pieces of the puzzle for the Texans' offense. That pairing has a great chance to supplement that playmaking ability and depth that has since been lost at the position without Noel, which wasn't quite as available just a few games ago.
In Weeks 2 and 3, the Texans' leading contributors at wide receiver while Nico Collins was sidelined with a hamstring strain were none other than Kayshon Boutte and Xavier Hutchinson. A little over a month later, now with Dell and Harrison Jr. as a part of the equation, Houston's fate at the position has taken a full 180.
The hurdle sitting between that playmaking really coming to fruition is for the Texans to find a way to get them on the field in longer stints. This past weekend against the Giants, the two failed to combine for more than 30 snaps on the offense , which is expected given their respective situations.
But that outcome could certainly change in a big way after the bye. Harrison Jr. will have another week of learning the Texans' playbook under his belt. Dell will be even more comfortable coming off of his knee injury and create a much more potent attack for Houston to lean on through the air.
When you add that pairing alongside an already bonafide top wideout like Nico Collins, there's more than enough reason to believe that the Texans' passing offense can stay steady, even without one of their most potent pass-catchers.
So of course, not having Noel on the field for the next two weeks is a noteworthy loss for the Texans, and takes away yet another high-potential receiver out of this offensive attack right next to his draft classmate in Jayden Higgins.
But if the Texans can continue to get Harrison Jr. and Dell involved in the game plan, and they hold up their end of the bargain, that'll be their best course of action in hopes that this offense can rebound moving forward. Time will tell if it'll come to fruition as expected.
